Katalog Berita (Halaman 19/57)

#7754. 18 Kitchen Hacks Our Readers Swear By

Family Handyman readers share smart solutions for everyday problems in the heart of your home.

From a surprising way to monitor power outages to an epic trick to double your Ziploc bags, Family Handyman readers share smart solutions for everyday problems in the heart of your home.

“The metal wheels of a refrigerator can scratch, dent or gouge just about any flooring surface. Laying down stiff cardboard or a piece of leftover carpet provides an effective barrier, but for the best protection, use a sheet of 1/8‑in. hardboard. The smooth surface protects floors and helps appliances slide into and out of place. —ANTHONY LOMBARDI

“To find out if power outages ruined the food in your freezer while you were away on vacation, freeze a container of water and rest a penny on top of the ice. If the penny is at the bottom when you get back, it means the power was off long enough to melt the water—as well as thaw (and likely spoil) everything in the freezer. —JOHN NAKAMURA

“If you don’t have a label handy, use a rubber band instead. Stretch it around your Mason jar, then write the contents with a permanent marker. The grippy rubber also makes the jar easier to open. —DAVID KOWALCZYK Picture Frame Message Board I wanted a nicer-looking place for my weekly grocery list and family notes, so I turned a picture frame into a dry-erase board. I simply cut decorative paper to fit the frame and put it behind the glass, creating a surface I can write on with a dryerase marker. —JESSIE DAWSON

“For a minor scorch mark on a laminate countertop, skip the abrasive cleaner. Buff it out with car wax or a mixture of toothpaste and baking soda instead.” —ELAINE WHITFIELD

“Leaky seals around faucets and sink rims can lead to slow but severe damage (they can destroy a countertop, for example). So after installing a new sink or faucet, dribble water around the area and wait a few minutes. Then get under the sink and look for leaks. —GREGORY PRITCHARD

“Sometimes it’s tough to mix foods such as old-fashioned oily peanut butter in a small jar by hand. But if you enjoy reaching for a power tool to solve a problem as I do, head out to the garage. As it turns out, the handle of a mixing spoon fits perfectly in the chuck of a cordless drill. —CLIFF MERCER

“Build a simple dispenser for your trash bags using 1/2-in. pipe and a few fittings. Screw a floor flange to the cabinet, thread in a 3-in.-long pipe nipple, and then thread a 90-degree elbow onto the nipple. Cut the vertical pipe so it’s a bit longer than the width of the roll of bags. Finally, thread the vertical piece into the elbow and slip on the roll.” —TRAVIS LARSON

“I turn sandwich-size bags into snack-size bags by heating up an old butter knife with a lighter and slicing the bag in half. The hot knife cauterizes the edges of the two new bags, and the cauterized edges are just as strong as the factory-sealed edges.” —JULIA TRENTON

“Need to sharpen a utility knife, pocket blade or scissors but don’t have a sharpening stone on hand? Flip a ceramic mug and use the unglazed ring on the bottom as a sharpener. Hold the blade at a 45-degree angle and slide it across the ring in one direction, from the base to the tip. This won’t replace a proper sharpening kit, but it can quickly clean up a dull edge in a pinch.” —RONALD ALVAREZ

“Ice packs are a great way to keep your lunch cool, but they can be expensive to replace if you tend to lose them. To make your own reusable version without spending a lot, soak a sponge in water, then place it in a small resealable plastic bag. Freeze it overnight, then pop it into your lunch container. As the ice melts, the bag holds the water until the sponge reabsorbs it. When you get home, simply refreeze the pack for next time. I like to keep several on hand to use in lunches and coolers, as well as for first aid. They’re inexpensive to make, easy to reuse and help reduce waste.” —TOM SHERIDAN

“Alphabetizing spices helps you quickly find what your recipe calls for and makes putting away jars just as fast. Another benefit? You can easily figure out which spices are missing from your pantry, so you’re less likely to discover you’re out of a key ingredient halfway through making a meal. Take a quick glance before grocery shopping to keep staples stocked.” —MARTIN SUTHERLAND

“When your favorite candle burns too low for a lighter or match to reach the wick, don’t risk burning your fingertips. Instead, light a piece of uncooked spaghetti. It is long enough to reach deep into tall candle holders and burns long enough to light the wick.” —PATRICIA HART

“For an extra-fresh garbage disposal, toss in a few lemon or lime peels. Run the disposal with cold water until you can’t hear any more grinding, then run it for another 30 seconds (with the water still on).” —GREGORY HOLT

“A countertop isn’t the best place to keep a recipe while you’re cooking. It takes up counter space, is difficult to read and is bound to get splattered. Instead, use a clothes hanger with pants clips to hang the recipe from a cabinet handle. Open the book or magazine to the desired page (or use a printout), clamp it in place and you have a simple hanging stand. This trick works best with smaller cookbooks, magazines or single-sheet recipes.” —GLENN WHITE

“My kitchen drawers used to be an absolute wreck, with pans and dishes crammed in however they’d fit. And seemingly every time I needed something, it was at the very bottom of the drawer. My solution was to cut a piece of 1/8-in. pegboard to the size of the drawer bottom and attach dowels using screws from underneath. Now my pans are organized and easy to access. The 10 minutes it took to build was easily made up with how much frustration it has saved me.” —JIM DAVIDSON

“Crawling under a kitchen sink to refill the soap dispenser was a hassle, so I tried filling it from above. But when I did, the soap formed an air-lock bubble and overflowed, creating a mess. That’s when I came up with the idea of inserting a drinking straw in the dispenser neck to relieve “bubble block.” Now when I refill the dispenser, the air escapes through the straw and the soap stays where it belongs.” —PAUL SNYDER

“A dishwasher makes quick work of disinfecting washable toys such as plastic building blocks. Drop the blocks in a mesh laundry bag and run your dishwasher as usual. Remove the bag before the drying cycle, letting the blocks air-dry on a towel. This method also works for items such as seashells, dish brushes, sponges and rags.” —ROBERT VALENTI

“If your refrigerator stops dispensing water after you change the filter, make sure the new filter is fully seated. Many people don’t twist it in completely, and one final turn may be all it takes to get the dispenser working again.” —STANLEY BEAUMONT

“An ironing board with the cover removed can be used as an extra cooling rack when you’re doing a lot of baking. Better yet, it frees up valuable counter space for other kitchen tasks. Just be sure to use pans, paper liners, parchment or some other barrier between baked goods and the board.” —LIZ GRABOWSKI

“When the rubber sink baffle on my garbage disposal gets grimy or starts to smell, I switch off the power at the breaker and scrub it with an old toothbrush dipped in hot, soapy water and baking soda. I lift the rubber flaps to clean underneath, where food and grime collect. Then I restore power, rinse it with cold water and run the disposal briefly to flush away the debris.” —CHARLES MCALLISTER

#7752. The Best Waterproof Gloves of 2026, Tested and Reviewed

Black Friday Deals Are Already Here ➡️ Tools, Generators, Essentials & More

By Mark Wolfe, Additional research provided by Tom Scalisi

Published Nov 21, 2026 9:00 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Like a rain jacket for your hands, waterproof gloves are essential gear for those working—or playing—outdoors in cold or inclement weather. For outdoor sports enthusiasts, they keep hands dry and protect against frostbite. For those who work outdoors, they are essential because they offer protection from grease, mud, and other wet messes.

We searched out a diverse collection of waterproof gloves for a wide variety of tasks in all seasons. Then we tested their ability to keep hands dry and comfortable in tough conditions. The Carhartt Waterproof Insulated Gloves earned our pick as the best waterproof gloves for men for their reliable waterproofing, comfortable insulation, and affordable price, and the MCTi Ski Gloves for Women topped our women’s picks for their watertight protection, flexible fit, and responsive touch-screen fingertips.

Bottom line: Discover the best waterproof gloves of 2026, tested for durability, comfort, and specific needs, ensuring dry and warm hands in any condition.

We initially selected the following gloves based on the quality of their construction, their durability, and the other features outlined previously. Then we tested them to discover how they held up under wet, slippery conditions. Find out how they performed in the reviews ahead.

Men looking for a long-lasting pair of gloves to keep their hands dry and warm may find what they’re looking for in Carhartt’s waterproof insulated gloves. From the shell to the liner to the palm pad, these gloves are made of 100 percent polyester. They provide a warm, durable, and waterproof barrier between the skin and the elements.

A liner made with Carhartt’s FastDry moisture-wicking technology prevents sweat from collecting inside the gloves, and a waterproof insert provides an extra layer of protection from the elements. Adjustable hook-and-loop closures and elastic cuffs keep hands snug while keeping out cold air and elements.

In our tests, these Carhartt waterproof work gloves were as comfortable as they were waterproof. They performed perfectly on all three of our waterproof tests. They stayed dry under the shower and when immersed in water while providing excellent holding ability thanks to the textured grip area. Three-dimensional construction lets the hand rest in a natural position and delivers good dexterity for gripping and holding. Although we didn’t test specifically for winter warmth, these gloves are deeply insulated for cold-weather work. However, the bulky profile takes away the ability to pick up small or thin items from a flat surface or to reach into a pants pocket.

What our tester says: “These got ‘Best Overall’ because they’re not only toasty and affordable, but they also make an excellent choice for winter chores while not looking like work gloves.”—Mark Wolfe, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the Carhartt waterproof gloves at Amazon.

Women on the hunt for warm, waterproof gloves may want to look at MCTi’s ski gloves. They pair a polyurethane outer shell with a faux leather palm and thumb-grip area for holding ski poles or other slippery objects. On the gloves’ interior, a waterproof liner helps keep moisture from reaching the skin.

MCTi’s gloves also contain 120 grams of Thinsulate insulation that keeps hands warm in temperatures as cold as -10 degrees Fahrenheit without adding much bulk. Handy elastic wrist leashes make keeping track of the gloves easier if the wearer removes them, and sensitive touch-screen pads on three fingers allow the wearer to answer a phone or send a text without having to take off the gloves.

In our tests, these ski gloves by MCTi seemed more like general-use winter gloves. The waterproof feature is on point, with zero water intrusion during testing and a capable grip in wet conditions. Not only that, but the insulation was less puffy than some of the other gloves we tested, which improved dexterity and flexibility for gripping and handling small items. The touch-screen fingertips worked well. Moreover, they’re available in an assortment of accent colors: gray, red, white, rose, and yellow.

Get the MCTi waterproof gloves at Amazon.

Men looking for lightweight protection from the weather may want to consider Ozero’s men’s thermal gloves, which provide warmth and weather resistance without a lot of bulk. These gloves feature a water-resistant and windproof polyester construction that keeps the wearer’s hands dry and warm in inclement weather (most of the shell fabric is indeed waterproof, but the seams and touch-screen pads on two fingers are not, hence the “water-resistant” designation). This pair is a good choice for cycling, running, walking, or other outdoor pursuits.

These gloves may not be well suited to subzero temperatures, but they’re suitable for regular winter wear and have some nice features. The gloves’ thumbs and index fingers contain sensors that are touch-screen compatible, and the palms are covered in grippy silica gel pods to help users maintain a good grip on phones and other belongings. Elastic cuffs keep out the elements. These gloves fit snugly; the manufacturer suggests sizing up for a more relaxed fit.

These mid-weight lifestyle gloves are built for everyday travel and tasks in frosty weather, but not in pouring rain. Our rain simulation and immersion tests revealed numerous water entry points. Water resistance was good in our aggressive rain simulation for about a minute before leaks developed, so we believe the gloves could keep hands mostly or completely dry during an average rainstorm. They provided excellent grip for wet items. The touch-screen feature worked well, and the snug, low-profile fit allowed us to pick up a key that was lying flat on a countertop. Also note that these gloves cost less than most of the others we tested. Moreover, they are slim and flexible and easily fit into jacket pockets.

Get the Ozero waterproof gloves at Amazon or Walmart.

Leather work gloves are a necessity when working near hot surfaces and sparks in addition to protecting the hands from abrasion, cuts, and punctures. Youngstown Glove Company’s FR Waterproof Leather Utility gloves incorporate both leather and Kevlar, a synthetic fabric commonly used for protection, along with a waterproof, windproof, breathable polyurethane barrier. These gloves, which have earned American National Standards Institute (ANSI) compliance for welding, provide Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA)-approved protection for a wide range of tasks. However, they don’t provide adequate protection for electrical work.

Youngstown’s waterproof utility work gloves delivered good waterproof and wet-grip performances in our three wet tests. Although we got the leather so thoroughly wet that the gloves became heavy, the waterproof barrier prevented water intrusion to the skin. Wet grip was not a problem. We were pleasantly surprised by the dexterity that these bulky gloves provided, thanks to their three-dimensional construction and a naturally relaxed hand posture. Overall, we would not recommend these gloves for extended use in a watery environment because those conditions would cause the leather to degrade quickly. However, those who need a sturdy and comfortable insulated glove for working in the elements may want to look at these.

Get the Youngstown waterproof gloves at Amazon, JB Tools, or Youngstown Glove Company.

Carhartt’s Cold Snap insulated work gloves offer both cold-weather protection and long-lasting construction that’s tough enough for the jobsite. With warm insulation on the outer shell and a reinforced palm, these polyester gloves are reinforced with leather for extra durability. They’re waterproof and have a nose wipe on the thumb, making them a good choice for working in rough weather.

Cold Snap gloves feature some of Carhartt’s proprietary materials, including a FastDry lining for wicking moisture and Storm Defender waterproofing treatment. They have a thick cuff with an adjustable drawstring for improved weather protection. A small section of goatskin around the finger and thumb area provides added grip.

Our second pair of Carhartt waterproof work gloves performed nearly as well as the first. It provided excellent waterproof and wet-grip performance along with excellent dexterity, considering the lofty insulation. The polyester and leather exterior sheds water very well instead of becoming saturated and heavy. We liked the drawcord cuff on these gloves a little less than we liked the hook-and-loop strap closure on our “Best Overall” selection because the barrel-cord tightener is harder to manipulate with gloved hands. Nevertheless, pairing outstanding waterproofing, warmth, and comfort with a great look is the winning recipe for an all-around great pair of gloves.

Get the Carhartt Cold Snap waterproof gloves on Amazon.

No more freezing hands when you try to take a pic or return an important text. These low-profile knitted Sealskinz gloves offer triple-layer insulated waterproof, windproof protection from the elements with touch-screen-capable fingertips and outstanding range of motion. The nylon and elastane outer layer offers excellent durability with silicone-printed grips on the palm and fingers for a secure grip. A mid-layer windproof, waterproof, breathable membrane keeps the warmth in and the elements out. The lining is made of merino wool, nylon, and elastane for added warmth and breathability.

These Sealskinz gloves offered a lot of things we really liked but a few things we didn’t. We appreciated that they were truly 100 percent waterproof, both in our simulated rain test and when immersed in water. They also offer outstanding wet-grip capability, with touch-perfect touch-screen functionality. The low-profile design, moderate amount of insulation, and superior wet performance are perfect for getting outside on those miserable raw days when it’s 30 degrees Fahrenheit with freezing rain. But we didn’t love the semi-absorbent exterior because it holds on to more than its share of water, even though the water never reached our hands. It makes these otherwise excellent gloves feel heavy and a little bit squelchy. However, these may be the best gloves when wet weather threatens.

Get the Sealskinz waterproof gloves at Amazon or Sealskinz.

Hestra’s Army Leather Heli Ski 3-Finger Gloves are designed for men and women who spend their time atop some of the coldest mountains. These three-finger gloves are constructed from Hestra’s windproof, breathable, and water-resistant Triton fabric, with goat leather on the palms and fingers for improved grip in cold and slippery conditions.

The insides of these Hestra gloves are made of a very thin polyester fiber with efficient insulating properties, which makes them warm without being overly bulky. The oversize cuffs feature a drawstring closure to keep out snow and moisture, and leashes ensure the gloves won’t get lost. These Army Leather Heli gloves are available in three colors.

These gloves looked great and performed better than expected in our tests, but they were not totally waterproof. We anticipated soaking-wet hands because of the leather and “water- resistant” fabric. In our tests, the leather eventually became wet, and some moisture from outside did seep inside. They offered an OK but not great grip when wet. The best advantages of these gloves are the finger configuration, which offers better warmth than a conventional glove and better articulation than a mitten. That said, we did not test for performance in cold weather. On the downside, the leather must be regularly oiled (a tube is included), and they take a long time to dry once wet.

Get the Hestra Heli waterproof gloves at Amazon, REI, or Backcountry.com.

Built in the style of traditional cuff-length work gloves, Hestra Job Titan Flex Gloves bring the outstanding comfort and durability of goatskin leather with waterproof neoprene cuffs and Hestra Flex fabric. The stress points on the palm and fingers are reinforced with double-layered leather, while the index fingers and thumbs feature touch-screen pads for convenience. These three-season work gloves are lined with moisture-wicking fleece for added warmth and comfort in cold, wet weather.

In our tests, these gloves provided good waterproof protection and excellent wet-gripping ability. They resisted water penetration for over a minute before moisture found its entry point at the edges of the touch-screen pad on the index finger. The touch-screen pad functioned well, and the glove offered good dexterity and comfort overall, but the sizing runs a bit small. The moderate price point and durable construction make them ideal spring, fall, or mild winter weather general-use work gloves.

Get the Hestra Titan waterproof gloves at Amazon.

We selected and tested a diverse assortment of waterproof gloves designed for a variety of uses in different seasons. For all of them, our key testing consideration was whether the gloves were truly waterproof. To find out, we used three testing methods and allowed the gloves to thoroughly dry between tests. All comments about sizing are subjective, based on sizing guides provided by the manufacturers and perceived comfort by the tester. On those gloves not listed as unisex, women tested women’s gloves, and men tested men’s gloves.

First, we simulated storm conditions with a rain-wand attachment on a garden hose. The testers wore each pair of gloves beneath a steady 2-minute shower, flexing their hands and turning them over to expose all parts of the gloves to the stream. In the second test, we immersed our gloved hands into a bucket of water, again flexing and rotating to ensure that they were completely wet. Finally, we tested them for wet-gripping ability while handling smooth wet stones. To merit inclusion in this guide, each pair of gloves passed all three tests with minimal water intrusion to the inside of the glove.

Before shopping for the best waterproof gloves, consider the type of work planned for the gloves as well as the kind of materials and construction desired. In this section, we review some key considerations to keep in mind while shopping for the best waterproof gloves, including materials, use, fit, and more.

Choosing the best waterproof gloves depends on how they’ll be used. Work gloves are completely different from those intended for outdoor sports or casual wear.

On garments labeled “waterproof,” the outer shell is usually where the magic happens. Materials like tightly woven nylon, polyester, softshell technical materials, treated leather, and others work well to shed water before it can seep through to the lining. Keep in mind that it’s very rare for leather gloves to actually be waterproof; more likely, they are simply water-resistant.

Aside from shell material, other elements in waterproof gloves’ exteriors make them useful in wet or messy situations. Some of the best waterproof gloves, for example, have textured grips that make it easier for the wearer to grab on to wet, slippery surfaces, making them ideal for skiing, cycling, and other active pursuits. Those looking for waterproof gloves for work may want to invest in gloves with reinforced palms and thumbs, which should last longer and stand up to more wear.

The best waterproof gloves contain an optional outer shell with conductors that transfer the electrical charge from a finger to a touch screen, allowing users to manipulate their phones without removing their gloves.

Some of the best waterproof gloves contain insulation that captures body heat, which forms air pockets that warm with the heat from the hand. Most insulation is a man-made poly-fill material such as Thinsulate or 3M.

To ensure gloves keep warm air inside and cold air from seeping in, some waterproof gloves have long elastic cuffs that hug tight to the wrist and arm, closing off any pathway for air to enter. For even warmer gloves, look for removable liners that can slip inside a waterproof glove to add another layer of insulation.

When selecting the best waterproof gloves, fit and comfort are essential. However, a “good fit” is relative to the activity. A pair of running gloves fits quite differently than a pair of winter work gloves or ski gloves.

Waterproof running or hiking gloves often feel like a stretchy, flexible second skin. Because they’re lightweight and wick away moisture, users sometimes forget they’re even wearing them.

Waterproof work gloves are bulkier and a bit stiff because they’re generally made from thick nylon or leather that resists ripping, tearing, and friction. Moreover, extra padding or reinforcement on the thumbs or palms can add to their bulk. Though work gloves fit loosely, they shouldn’t be so loose that it’s difficult to pick up small items while wearing them.

Ski gloves are flexible but don’t wear particularly well because they’re typically made from materials like nylon. Properly fitting ski gloves fit snugly around the wrist but are roomy enough to allow the skier to manipulate straps on ski poles and boot bindings.

Also consider breathability. If hands sweat and moisture collects inside the glove, it won’t matter that the shell is waterproof because hands will still get wet. Breathable gloves help some of the heat and moisture escape without letting in cold outer air and moisture.

Now that you know a bit more about the factors to consider when choosing the best waterproof gloves for your needs, some questions may remain. The following are some of the most frequently asked questions about the best waterproof gloves, so check for an answer to your question below.

Waterproof means that absolutely no water makes its way into the glove. Water-resistant means that the gloves shed water to a degree before water comes in.

As one of the best options for the warmest waterproof gloves, the Carhartt Cold Snap waterproof gloves are warm enough to protect your hands in very cold temperatures.

You can wash some waterproof gloves, but it’s best to spot clean them and use a boot dryer with a glove attachment if they become soiled.

The best way to dry the inside of waterproof gloves is to put them on a boot dryer with a glove attachment.

After months of scouring the market and putting products through their paces, we’ve named the best of the best in new tools. There’s something for everyone, from veteran pros to average Joes.

#7751. The Reason Some Parking Lots Have Angled Spaces Instead of Straight Ones

Angled parking spaces aren't just a design choice. Their layout can make turning easier, control traffic, and change how a lot uses space.

Navigating a new parking lot can be confusing and stressful. Some have one-way traffic, some have different parking rules. Even the parking spaces themselves can vary, with some lots using straight spaces and others using diagonal parking spaces. It turns out that small difference is intentional.

Parking lot designers think about how vehicles enter spaces, where drivers back out, and how much room cars need between rows. Learn why some parking lots use diagonal spaces, how the layout affects traffic, and what drivers should watch for.

Diagonal parking spaces are easier to pull into because drivers don’t have to make as sharp a turn. This is especially helpful in busy lots where cars are frequently coming and going. These spaces usually face one-way lanes, allowing drivers to pull in from the same direction. This helps keep traffic moving and reduces the chance of cars approaching each other head-on.

Drivers still need to follow the arrows, though. Entering from the wrong direction makes it harder to pull into a space and can put drivers in the path of cars backing out.

Not always. According to the Iowa Statewide Urban Design and Specifications, “One-way angled parking provides fewer spaces than perpendicular for the same length of aisle.”

The benefit is that one-way angled parking allows for narrower driving lanes, since drivers don’t need as much room to turn. Two-way angled parking is also possible, though Iowa’s guidelines say it’s generally less efficient than other layouts.

There’s also a downside to consider. Backing out of an angled space can be difficult when neighboring cars block the view, especially larger trucks and SUVs.

Some streets use back-in angled parking to address this problem. Drivers back into a space so they can pull forward when leaving. According to the University of Kentucky, Kentucky Transportation Center, “With the front of their vehicle facing the street, a motorist has improved sight distance when leaving a parking space.”

Back-in parking also lets passengers get out toward the sidewalk and keeps loading and unloading away from traffic. For regular diagonal spaces, drivers should back out slowly and watch for approaching cars and pedestrians. Backup cameras can help, but they shouldn’t replace checking the surrounding area.

#7749. Social Media Platforms Not Liable for Racist Buffalo Mass Shooting, Says N.Y. High Court by 4-3 Vote

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

But a majority of the judges seem to endorse liability for "addictive design" in other cases (which wouldn't involve liability for spreading particular viewpoints).

From the 4-judge unsigned majority opinion in Patterson v. Meta Platforms, Inc., decided today by N.Y.'s high court:

On May 14, 2022, a man motivated by heinous white supremacist ideologies he allegedly adopted due to content he viewed on social media carried out a mass shooting at a Buffalo grocery store, killing 10 and injuring three others. Plaintiffs, victims of the shooting and their family members, commenced these actions against the shooter's parents, firearms manufacturers, and social media companies, seeking compensation for their injuries.

These appeals concern motions to dismiss plaintiffs' claims against several social media companies whose platforms the shooter allegedly used before committing this unspeakable act of violence. Specifically, plaintiffs contend that their complaints state causes of action for products liability based on defective features of these social media defendants' platforms and their failure to warn thereof….

[P]laintiffs failed to adequately plead that features of [the] social media defendants' products proximately caused their injuries. Generally, a defendant's acts qualify as a proximate cause when they are "a substantial cause of the events which produced the injury." This inquiry examines

"the foreseeability of the event resulting in injury; the passage of time between the originally negligent act and the intervening act; the spatial gap, if any, between the original act and the intervening act; whether the original act of negligence was a completed occurrence or was ongoing at the time of the intervening act; whether and, if so, what other forces combined to bring about the harm; as well as public policy considerations regarding the scope of liability."

Foreseeability is often the most significant factor. Indeed, if an unforeseeable intervening criminal act of a third party causes the plaintiff's injury, the causal connection is severed. Thus, proximate causation will not be found when the intervening act "is extraordinary under the circumstances, not foreseeable in the normal course of events, or independent of or far removed from the defendant's conduct." "Although foreseeability and proximate cause are generally questions for the factfinder, there are instances in which proximate cause can be determined as a matter of law because 'only one conclusion may be drawn from the established facts'" such as when "the original negligent act merely 'furnished the occasion for'—but did not cause—'an unrelated act to cause injuries not ordinarily anticipated.'"

Here, plaintiffs failed to adequately allege that the remaining social media defendants' product defects proximately caused the shooter to carry out the mass shooting that resulted in plaintiffs' injuries. The complaints, even accepting the factual allegations as true, fail to establish that the shooter's actions were a natural and foreseeable consequence of these defendants' decisions about how to design and operate their platforms.

Instead, under the circumstances, the shooter's actions were so extraordinary as to sever the causal chain as a matter of law. {Our conclusion is limited to the unusual facts of this case, where the platforms' assertedly addictive features were alleged to have harmed the shooter rather than the plaintiffs directly.} We therefore need not address the scope of section 230 of the Communications Decency Act or how it would apply to the claims against these defendants.

Judge Halligan joined the majority, but also wrote a concurring opinion:

I join the majority because I agree that the plaintiffs have not adequately pleaded proximate causation. I write separately to underscore that, for me, this conclusion rests squarely on the highly unusual facts presented here, and to offer some additional thoughts regarding the scope of section 230.

As an initial matter, I agree with my dissenting colleagues that the plaintiffs alleged that several of the defendants tortiously designed addictive products. The complaints make a number of general claims about social media and youth: that defendants' platforms are addictive; that compulsive use of social media, particularly by young people, causes emotional disturbance and "impulsive decision-making and risk-taking behavior"; and that such use can also yield other deleterious consequences, including "sleep disturbances, mental health problems and suicidal ideation, and violent, hateful acts." The complaints further assert that the social media defendants, knowing of the addictive quality of their products and the heightened susceptibility of young users, not only failed to implement features for limiting use or warning parents, but also took deliberate advantage of that vulnerability by utilizing "strategic timing and clustering of notifications to lure back users" and by implementing "barriers to the deactivation and deletion of accounts." …

I find the claims before us quite distinct from the cases cited by the dissent that have allowed products liability claims premised on the addictiveness of social media platforms to proceed. I have little doubt that a plaintiff could allege a sufficient connection between the design of a platform and adverse consequences for the mental health of young users. In those cases, the harms that form the basis for the claims—for example, the alleged inducement of "compulsive use among young users to the detriment of their health and well-being"—flow directly from the platforms' allegedly defective features, leaving little question "that the defective design was a substantial factor in causing plaintiff's injury."

But the plaintiffs here are not bringing a claim on behalf of users. Instead, they are seeking recompense for the victims of a crime committed by a social media user. In other words, the allegedly addictive properties of the platforms were not alleged to have harmed the plaintiffs here directly, but rather to have harmed the shooter, who in turn engaged in extensive research and planning before murdering ten people and wounding others…. I do not see the connection between the two as sufficiently articulated to allow the case to proceed.

Three aspects of these claims inform my conclusion. First, although intervening criminal acts do not necessarily sever the causal chain, the shooter's conduct was apparently painstakingly planned and extraordinarily violent.

Second, the prominence of content in many of plaintiffs' allegations gives me real pause. Even if we were to interpret section 230 as not immunizing defendants against claims for actions that rest, at least in part, on content, I am not aware of other instances where a court has held that provocative content proximately caused someone to commit a violent crime, and I am hesitant to take that step here. {I understand the plaintiffs to disclaim on appeal any effort to base liability on defendants' roles as publishers of content. But their complaints can be read to allege that the platforms are defective at least in part because of the racist and extremist content they make available, and the plaintiffs acknowledge that content is a necessary link in the causal chain leading to their harms.}

Third, the defendants' platforms have billions of worldwide users. To the extent that proximate cause could rest on a correlation between social media use and a specific type of harmful act committed by any one of those users, the potential liability would sweep broadly, to say the least. If all such conduct were "a natural and foreseeable consequence" of a platform's design choices, the concept of proximate cause would have little meaning….

As for section 230, …. "we [have] read section 230 to bar 'lawsuits seeking to hold a service provider liable for its exercise of a publisher's traditional editorial functions.'" … Our endorsement of a "traditional editorial functions" test for section 230 immunity, however, does little to answer whether the conduct of modern social media platforms can be labelled such a function.

As to claims that a defendant designed its platform features to encourage or facilitate addiction, irrespective of the particular content promoted by the platform, I agree with the dissent that they are not barred by section 230. That is because such conduct does not constitute a traditional editorial function, even under a broad understanding of that term.

As to claims that challenge a social media platform's use of content-recommendation algorithms, the dissent appears to take the view that content-recommendation algorithms which are designed to be addictive are not covered by section 230 immunity, since they increase engagement in a way that could not have been envisioned at the time that provision was enacted in 1996. I have no quarrel with how we framed the scope of section 230 in Shiamili: the key question is whether a platform engaged in a traditional editorial function, akin to a decision "to publish, withdraw, postpone or alter content." But whether platforms' use of content-recommendation algorithms can be said to resemble traditional decisions to publish, withdraw, postpone, or alter content is, for me, a more difficult question….

[O]verly broad interpretations of section 230 in the face of a rapidly changing technological landscape are unmoored from Congress's purpose in enacting that provision—to protect minors from being exposed to pornography online…. Given that caution, I would not be inclined to extend section 230's reach to all content-recommendation algorithms. I am particularly skeptical that use of individualized content-recommendation algorithms—that is, algorithms that "assess[ ] a user's prior posts, friends, or viewing habits to recommend new content and connections"—constitutes a traditional publisher function. After all, "[t]raditional publication has never included selecting the news, opinion pieces, or classified ads to send to each individual reader based on guesses as to their preferences and interests." Instead, such functions may be "more analogous to the actions of a direct marketer, matchmaker, or recruiter than to those of a publisher."

In my view, a closer question is presented as to engagement-maximizing algorithms that, unlike the algorithms described above, do not take into account any individual user's conduct but instead seek to "promote[ ] third-party content" based on "cumulative user engagement." On one hand, algorithms that do not respond to individual user conduct may be thought to resemble a publisher's traditional aim of presenting content that users, on the whole, want to see. On the other hand, one might conclude that "generic" content-based algorithms bear no more resemblance to traditional publication than their "'advanced'—individualized—counterparts" because they still rely on an assessment of user viewing habits in a manner akin to "a direct marketer" rather than a traditional publisher. My dissenting colleagues offer yet another variation on this point; they assert that engagement-maximizing algorithms differ from an editor's choice of where to place a news story because the algorithms are "designed to prey on neurological frailties and alter brain chemistry."

Whether section 230 protects any of these algorithms is, for me, a difficult question, and I do not think the record before us sheds much light on how different types of content-recommendation algorithms actually operate on the social media defendants' individual platforms—information that might affect my view. We need not decide those questions today because, whatever the scope of the "traditional editorial functions" protected by section 230, the plaintiffs have failed to sufficiently allege that the defendants' platforms' features caused their grave injuries.

Judge Rivera, joined by Chief Judge Wilson and Judge Troutman, dissented in relevant part; an excerpt from the very long opinion:

The complaints detail the shooter's transformation from a seemingly ordinary teenager into a virulent racist and violent white supremacist…. [In his manifesto, t]he shooter also wrote that he "was not born racist nor [did he] gr[o]w up to be racist." Rather, he was exposed to and indoctrinated in his ideology of racial violence after using various social media platforms, starting with Instagram, YouTube, and Snapchat in his early teen years, before he transitioned to more niche platforms like Reddit, Discord, Twitch and 4chan. The shooter claimed he quickly "became transfixed with and addicted to [the] online world." He wrote in his diary:

"I'm addict[ed] to consoooooming. It's 2 in the morning. w[hat] t[he] f[*ck] … I'll admit my mental health has seriously degraded these past few years, especially in the last few months. I should be sleeping right now. I'm just browsing online:/" (emphasis added).

By his own account, he sacrificed "years of [his] life" to being online, often "stay[ing] up late" "browsing Reddit or watching YouTube" "every day." He stated that his compulsive social media use "seriously degraded" his mental health and isolated him from his peers. Rather than "go[ing] to friend's houses" or other social gatherings, "[e]very day after school [he] would just go home and play games and watch YouTube, mostly by [him]self." Ultimately, as he descended further into isolation, he believed he had no other choice but to commit this barbarous act.

Plaintiffs allege that the shooter's experience of compulsive social media engagement is widespread because the products' addictive features are fundamental to the social media defendants' business model. According to plaintiffs, defendants' business models seek to maximize user engagement through products "designed to be addictive." Plaintiffs assert that the operation of these products on the shooter, and their adverse impact on his mind caused by their addictive features, are links in the proximate causal chain underlying plaintiffs' tort liability causes of action against the social media defendants….

The Appellate Division erroneously concluded that defendants are immune from plaintiffs' lawsuit under Section 230. As I discuss, Section 230 does not shield defendants from plaintiffs' products liability and failure to warn allegations grounded on allegedly addictive products, as those claims have nothing to do with defendants' role as a third-party content publisher or as the creator of protected speech….

To the extent plaintiffs' claims against the social media defendants are based upon defendants' publication of third-party content, including racist, white supremacist, and violent content, defendants are immune from suit pursuant to Section 230. However, not all claims asserted in the complaints are based upon defendants' publication of third-party content. Rather, as I explain, the complaints also stated causes of action based on defendants' design of allegedly defective products and failure to warn….

Plaintiffs assert that these defendants are civilly liable for their role in addicting the shooter to social media and consequent deterioration of his mental health. Plaintiffs' complaints set forth the entire chain of causation that allegedly led to the mass shooting. By designing highly addictive algorithms known to cause severe mental harm to teenagers—like the shooter—the social media defendants created a direct link to the resulting damages, particularly given their failure to warn users and parents of these risks…. [T]here is no Section 230 immunity that attaches to the architecture of defendants' social media products—particularly their purposefully addictive algorithms….

Defendants' alternative argument that the complaints were properly dismissed on First Amendment grounds is unpersuasive. At this pre-answer stage of the litigation, it is unclear how precisely the content-recommendation algorithms function, meaning it is not possible to determine, as a matter of law, on a motion to dismiss that the algorithms themselves are protected speech. That determination requires factual findings dependent on future discovery. On a motion to dismiss we only decide whether the plaintiffs' claim is cognizable and not whether it will eventually succeed based on the facts established by the record….

And here's a short excerpt from the dissent's long discussion of why it rejects the majority's proximate cause theory:

The majority's conclusion that plaintiffs "fail to establish that the shooter's actions were a natural and foreseeable consequence" of the social media defendants' platforms because "the shooter's actions were so extraordinary as to sever the causal chain as a matter of law" is unsupported by our well-established tort liability doctrines. First, we have made clear that there may be more than one link in a causal chain and there may be more than one tortfeasor liable, jointly or individually, for a plaintiff's injuries. "[T]he mere fact that other persons share some responsibility for [the] plaintiff's harm does not absolve [a] defendant from liability." Thus, the fact that the third-party content creators may bear responsibility for the harm does not mean that defendants bear none.

Second, a defect need only be a "substantial cause"—not the sole cause—"of the events which produced the injury." Substantial means more than slight or trivial. Plaintiffs' allegations that defendants' product adversely affected the shooter's mental health and behavior, making him a compulsive social media user, with the attendant negative impact on his mind and body, isolated from others, rendering him more susceptible to commit this horrific violent act, easily satisfies the "substantial cause" standard.

Third, not all intervening acts break the causal chain. An intervening act only breaks the causal nexus if it is extraordinary under the circumstances, unforeseeable in the normal course of events, or independent of and far removed from the defendant's conduct. That determination depends on whether the intervening act and its consequences were the foreseeable result of a defendant's tortious conduct. Even the "intentional" or "criminal" intervening acts of a third party can be reasonably foreseeable….

[W]hile here, the harm arose from exposure to graphic violence and white supremacist propaganda, plaintiffs allege that the algorithm is content-agnostic. According to plaintiffs, defendants' products and platforms rely on these complex algorithms to keep users engaged, which negatively impacts young people's mental health, and, in turn, increases the tendency to violent behavior, all the while driving revenue for these defendants. Thus, the majority's assertion that the shooter's actions were not foreseeable is nothing more than a factual conclusion, but that determination cannot be made by the Court on a motion to dismiss….

Eric A. Shumsky, Moez M. Kaba, and Lisa LeCours are listed as representing the platforms.

#7748. Crucial Snow Blower Maintenance Tasks to Complete Before the First Snow

Black Friday Deals Are Already Here ➡️ Tools, Generators, Essentials & More

Published Nov 21, 2026 10:00 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

Imagine your frustration when your driveway is covered in snow after the first winter storm, but your snow blower won’t start. As winter approaches, it’s time to make sure your snow blower is ready to tackle that first snowfall. You’ll want to take a few steps to check that it’s tuned up and ready to go without a hitch. We spoke to Sean Dwyer, senior product manager for commercial and residential wheeled products at Husqvarna Group North America to identify the top snow blower maintenance tasks to prioritize so you are prepared when the first snowflake falls.

By far the most important step is to make sure you have a fresh supply of fuel, says Dwyer. “If you have regular pump fuel, it should be less than 30 days old, and ideally premium grade that’s a non-ethanol blend,” he explains. Fuel can go stale over time and gum up the snow blower’s carburetor. Dwyer recommends running the unit out of gas before storing it. “Otherwise, at a minimum, purchase stabilized canned fuel or add a fuel stabilizer.” Gasoline with a stabilizer typically lasts for about 4 to 6 months.

Spend some time reviewing the key components of the unit. “This means checking engine oil and tire pressures, and also starting the unit to ensure proper wheel drive and auger operation,” notes Dwyer. “This is also a good time to shut the fuel off and run the carburetor dry to give your snow blower the best chance of a successful operation when you need it.”

In addition, pay attention to these additional parts of the snow blower:

Featuring an easy-to-pour package and effective formula, this motor oil washes dirt and deposits out of the engine as it passes through.

Battery-powered snow blowers are convenient, but it’s important to recognize that cold weather and batteries don’t typically work well together, warns Dwyer. Checking battery health is part of regular snow blower maintenance. Rechargeable batteries can degrade over time, and won’t be able to hold as much charge as they age as they do when new. He recommends keeping fully charged batteries in the house or a location where they will remain above freezing temperatures. “If everything is in the cold garage, there is a good chance they won’t work when you need them to,” he explains. “Also, remember that when you are done, bring the batteries back to a warm place so they are ready to go next time.”

Snow blowers typically contain shear bolts (also called pins) as a safety feature. The shear bolts are designed to break to protect the auger gears from damage if the unit runs into hard objects like ice from a blizzard. There is typically one pin on each auger and one or two on the impeller.

To change these components, wear protective gloves. “With the engine shut off, try to rotate each individual auger by hand,” says Dwyer. “You should not be able to rotate the augers, and the shear bolts will be visually present.” To check the impeller, look for the shear bolts, or hold one of the augers firmly, and slowly try to turn the impeller. “Be careful when checking the impeller, as it is tied to the shaft that will drive the augers.”

If these items spin freely, the shear bolt is likely damaged or missing, says Dwyer. Replace any missing or broken bolts to protect your snow blower. It’s a good idea to always keep a stash of shear bolts on hand.

Designed to wear down with use, skid shoes help keep a snow blower’s housing at the correct height and also protect your pavement. They are located on the lower sides of the auger housing and are designed to hold the scraper, located at the bottom of the auger housing, just above the ground, says Dwyer. “As these shoes wear, the scraper will contact the ground and wear will increase,” he explains.

“A simple way to adjust the shoes is to sit the snow blower scraper on something around ¼ inch thick, like a paint stir stick, and then loosen the bolts holding the shoes to adjust them down to contact the ground and retighten,” suggests Dwyer.

#7746. 7 Surfaces You Should Never Use Ice Melt On

Avoid damaging salt-sensitive outdoor surfaces with these expert-backed suggestions.

Ice melt salt is an effective option for preventing and removing ice from sidewalks, driveways and stairs, but it isn’t suitable for every surface. Applying ice melt to certain materials can cause significant damage and should be avoided. Ahead, learn which surfaces are most vulnerable to damage from ice melt, why it happens and what safer alternatives you can use to keep outdoor areas free from ice.

Ice melt salt chemically reacts with certain materials, accelerates freeze-thaw cycles and alters surface moisture levels to cause damage. The type of damage will depend on the surface and how it interacts with ice melt.

Ice melt contains rock salt, calcium chloride and/or magnesium chloride to melt ice faster and at lower temperatures. While all melting salt is corrosive and can damage outdoor surfaces, ice melt products can react differently than rock salt alone.

Ice melt seeps deeply into porous cement-based materials. The calcium chloride in ice melt can react with elements of concrete or brick to form calcium oxychloride crystals. As the crystals grow, they generate extreme pressure that can cause cracks, surface spalling and crumbling.

De-icing products accelerate freeze-thaw cycles in porous cement-based surfaces, causing them to break down. “It makes the freezing and thawing cycle more aggressive, which is what causes the surface to break up,” Murphy says.

Though less damaging than rock salt, ice melt can still contribute to deterioration. Calcium chloride and magnesium chloride attract and retain moisture, increasing the potential for freeze-thaw damage.

Conversely, ice melt draws moisture out of organic materials, causing them to dry out. Over time, this moisture loss can lead to warping, cracking, splitting and other forms of deterioration.

Ice melt accelerates metal oxidation to create rust. It can corrode rebar embedded in concrete, potentially causing cracks and structural damage, as well as rusting exposed metal stairs and railings.

It’s best to avoid applying salt to these salt-sensitive surfaces.

“New concrete is the most vulnerable because it takes weeks to fully cure, so salt on the surface will cause the top few millimeters to flake off,” Murphy says. To be safe, avoid salting new concrete for the first season.

“Cracked concrete opens up for water to get inside, and salt in the water will only make that worse because it will freeze and thaw more aggressively,” Murphy says.

All ice melt products will damage hard-scape surfaces due to chemical reactions and freeze-thaw cycles. “If you are using them, use them sparingly and remove them as soon as possible to decrease continuous exposure for your hardscape areas,” Zurcher says.

Natural stone like limestone and flagstone can react to ice melt compounds. The porous surface is vulnerable to damaging freeze-thaw cycles as well.

Harsh de-icers can damage dyed, painted or stamped concrete surfaces by breaking down color pigments.

Metal stairs and railings will rapidly rust when salt is applied to them, so it’s best to avoid it.

Ice melt draws moisture from wood, causing cracking, warping and raised fibers. It also degrades paint and stain and leaves behind chalky white salt stains.

Sand: Sand doesn’t melt ice, but does provide traction to prevent slips.

Wood ash: Instead of throwing away wood ash, use it as a salt alternative to melt ice and also provide improved traction.

Electric mats: Installed before cold weather sets in, electric melting mats warm up and prevent ice from ever forming. These can be very effective on stairs and sidewalks.

Weed torch: Weed torches are handy when you need to melt a lot of ice quickly. Do not use one to melt ice on wood and avoid painted or stained concrete as well.

“The best way to reduce damage from these chemicals is to shovel snow as soon as possible,” Zurcher says, so you can use less of them. Use ice melt sparingly, and only as directed. A handful is enough to treat three square yards. Instead of using ice melt alone, mix a small amount with sand to treat surfaces.

Regular sealing protects cement-based products.  “Reseal every three to five years to make sure no water can get in, salty or not,” Murphy says. Additionally, use chloride-free de-icing products, or those labelled as “concrete-safe”.

Newly poured concrete is the most vulnerable to salt damage, but all concrete surfaces will experience damage with enough prolonged exposure to salt.

It depends on the extent of the damage. Major cracks and breakage mean concrete needs to be removed and repoured, Zurcher says, while surface damage could be skim-coated, with potentially limited results.

Pet-safe products will have similar effects on hardscape areas, Zurcher says, as they still contain salt.

#7743. Who supervises the system? Agentic AI and the future of lawyer oversight

For two years, the legal profession’s artificial intelligence conversation has centered on an attorney asking a system a question and checking its answer. That is no longer enough.

Systems entering legal practice perform work: taking in a matter, researching, drafting motions, and choosing their own next steps. Used well, they can reduce routine work, freeing lawyers for judgment and client advice.

The profession built its supervision framework around people and bounded tools. An agentic system fits neither model: It has no license to lose or judgment to train, yet acts across a workflow with autonomy the Model Rules do not squarely address.

When AI moves from answering questions to executing multistep legal workflows, what does meaningful human oversight look like?

The unit of supervision is no longer an answer; it is a system of delegated decisions.

The ABA Model Rules of Professional Conduct anticipated part of this shift. In 2012, the ABA changed Rule 5.3’s title from “Responsibilities Regarding Nonlawyer Assistants” to “Responsibilities Regarding Nonlawyer Assistance.” Its comments encompassed technology-enabled services; a companion resolution added technological competence to what became Comment 8 of Rule 1.1. In 2024, Formal Opinion 512 applied Rules 1.1, 5.1, and 5.3 to lawyers’ use of generative AI and their supervision of the people and providers using it.

That guidance remains organized around a tool: review its output, protect client information, train users and assess providers. It offers less direction when the system executes the workflow, deciding which documents to pull, which facts matter, and what goes where—decisions the finished product may not reveal. Reviewing only the output confirms the car arrived, not its route. Supervision of output is not supervision of process.

METR’s May 2026 report sharpens the point. Assessing agents inside frontier developers (or entities that train AI models), it found them exceeding intended bounds and misleading users about their work, especially on difficult tasks. It did not study law firm deployments, and routine monitoring might have caught every incident because an independent record existed. The lesson: A lawyer cannot treat an agent’s account as the record of its work. That account is another output of the same probabilistic process, which has training incentives that can reward telling users what they want to hear. Asking the agent to double-check itself is not an independent control.

Accountability cannot rest solely with whoever pressed “run.” It must be institutional and individual, extending to those who designed, approved and maintained the workflow. Every deployed workflow should have a named lawyer-owner authorized to pause it, just as every matter has a responsible partner. This does not displace the matter lawyer’s responsibilities. The owner’s authority must permit suspension on suspicion alone before a committee convenes or a vendor responds. Ownership without it is a label.

Final output review remains necessary. Oversight must also cover consequential junctures: privilege calls, external communications, filings and anything irreversible or beyond client authorization. Supervision begins at design time: deciding what a workflow may do independently, its latitude to reason, and where it must stop and ask. Every firm should be able to answer: Where can this system act without a human seeing it first, and who decided that?

A tested record on comparable work can justify less intensive routine checking, though never at those consequential junctures. Greater autonomy should be approved and recorded. Material changes to the model, tools, permissions or workflow should trigger reassessment and renewed authorization.

Autonomy bundles three permissions requiring separate calibration: generating work product, accessing sensitive information, and acting in firm or client systems. Permissions should narrow as consequences grow: broad room to draft; matter-scoped room to read; and narrow, logged room to act. A first-year may draft the memo; nobody gives them unilateral wire authority. The grant of action is never implied by the grant of access.

If a firm cannot trace what a system did, it cannot supervise it; where reasoning cannot be audited, behavior must be. Otherwise, recordkeeping, preservation, and verification of representations to clients, courts, and third parties may suffer. Three mechanisms matter: an audit trail independent of the agent’s reporting, means to interrupt workflows mid-run, and a path to unwind reversible actions—with honesty about those that cannot be reversed. Record model versions and configurations too: Providers update continuously, and a workflow validated in March may differ from August’s.

Five workflows can be governed individually; 500 cannot. Solo and small practices may use a simple inventory but still need a way to stop a workflow. At scale, governance becomes operational infrastructure: an inventory of deployed systems, risk classification, approval gates, monitoring and reassessment. The profession knows this playbook: Ask a managing partner how conflicts are governed, and you will hear about a system, not a policy.

Delay accumulates governance debt: workflows deployed faster than they can be inventoried, permissions granted faster than they can be reviewed. Like all debt, it compounds quietly. When data-protection regimes preceded settled enforcement guidance, prudent organizations built from regulatory intent rather than waiting for caselaw. Agentic AI presents the same problem: established duties but no settled operating model.

Ownership, calibrated oversight, permission limits, traceability, reversibility and governance at scale matter wherever organizations deploy agentic AI. What distinguishes law is that our supervisory duties are explicit and long-standing. We are not a special case. We are an early test case.

Fortunately, the test is familiar. Lawyers have been supervising work they did not personally perform since the first associate billed their first hour. The question is no longer only whether lawyers can use AI competently. It is whether we can supervise systems that increasingly do the work of the supervised.

Scott A. Meyers is the chairman and CEO, and Michael Adler is the director of artificial intelligence governance and data protection at Akerman, an Am Law 100 law firm.

Editor’s Note: In preparing the content, the authors used generative AI tools under their direction and supervision and provide the following description of the manner and extent of that use. The article’s thesis, argument and conclusions are the authors’ own: the delegation-of-authority in the legal profession framework originated with the authors, who selected or approved every source cited. Working from the authors’ instructions, outlines and source materials, AI tools were used to generate and revise draft text; to condense the manuscript to the ABA Journal’s length and format requirements; to perform supplementary research at the authors’ direction; and to check quotations, figures and citations against their primary sources. The authors directed the revisions, made line edits in their own hand, independently reverified the cited figures against the primary sources, and reviewed and approved every sentence of the final Content. No AI-generated text was included in the content without author review, and the authors remain responsible for the content.

#7742. My New Book Chapter on How to Curb Dangerous Emergency Powers

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Now avaialble on SSRN. It is coauthored with Josh Braver, and will be published in the forthcoming Cato Handbook on Executive Power.

My forthcoming chapter on "Emergency Powers" is now available on SSRN. It is coauthored with Josh Braver (University of Wisconsin), and will be published in the forthcoming Cato Handbook on Executive Power, edited by Molly Nixon. Braver is a leading expert on the law of domestic use of the military and a liberal/progressive. I am a a libertarian. If we can come to agreement on these issues, I hope others can, as well. Here is the abstract:

Emergency powers are special types of government authorities that are only supposed to be used under extraordinary circumstances, in order to address a crisis. But, over time, many have become institutionalized as near-blank checks that the executive can invoke at will. This situation imperils civil liberties and our constitutional system.

This chapter goes over the major US emergency powers, including the National Emergencies Act, the Insurrection Act, the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA), and others, and offers proposals for curbing the dangers they create. Effective reform requires a combination of new legislation and strong, nondeferential judicial review.

I recently covered related issues in an article for Just Security, which goes over potential legislative reforms. In the Cato Handbook chapter, Braver and I cover both legislative reforms and how judicial review can be strengthened.

#7741. The Safest Way to Shovel Snow, According to Experts

Avoid injury with these expert-backed snow shoveling safety tips.

With autumn in full swing, it’s time to start thinking about preparing for the looming winter months. If you live in a snow-prone climate, this means getting out the shovels, salt and snowblower before the first flakes fly. Even if you’re not new to shoveling, it’s worth learning how to do it safely, as injuries can occur at any time.

Shoveling may seem simple, but can lead to strains, pulls and cardiac events if not done properly. Ahead, learn expert-backed tips to shovel snow the right (and safe) way with insights from cardiologist Dr. Bradley Serwer.

The safest way to shovel snow is to push it as much as possible and avoid lifting. If you must lift snow to remove it, bend at the knees and lift with your legs instead of your back.

“The most important tool when preparing to shovel snow is good common sense,” Serwer says. “Dress appropriately and consider the risks of the job at hand.”

Dress in layers that allow you to remove or open up a layer of clothing as you warm up to avoid getting overheated. Opt for a moisture wicking base layer, a mid-weight layer and a jacket that is wind-resistant and waterproof. Wear warm, waterproof gloves, a hat, warm socks and thick-soled winter boots. For particularly cold temperatures and high winds, add ski goggles and a balaclava to protect sensitive facial skin.

Consider a quick warm up and stretch session for a safer shoveling session. Get your blood pumping with some light activity like jumping jacks, walking in place or climbing up and down the stairs in your home.  Gently stretch major muscle groups before heading outside.

Snow shovels are not all created equal. For safer shoveling, choose one that is less demanding on your back, joints and heart. Ergonomic shovels feature a curved handle that reduces back strain when lifting. Snow plow shovels are meant to push snow only, not lift it. And battery-powered shovels act like mini-snowblowers to quickly remove snow without any manual input.

Keep your back straight, bend at the knees and use your legs to lift snow for safer shoveling. Keep the loaded shovel close to your body, then, without twisting, turn your body toward the direction you place the snow. If snow is wet or deeper than six inches, remove it in smaller layers, rather than one heavy shovelful.

“It is often underestimated what kind of physical workload is required to shovel a substantial amount of snow,” Serwer says. That’s why it’s important to pace yourself, stop regularly and plan ahead to avoid overexertion. Opt for a slow and steady pace, especially if you’re typically sedentary. Rigorous snow shoveling will quickly lead to overexertion and cardiac strain. Going slow allows you to focus on safe shoveling technique, preventing possible muscle strains and pulls. Stay well-hydrated when shoveling and take regular breaks to allow your heart rate to return to normal and your muscles to recover.

Stop shoveling if you’re experiencing cardiac distress, cold-related conditions, dehydration or back strain.

“Shoveling snow can be a very strenuous activity, placing notable strain on the cardiovascular system,” Serwer says. Know the signs of a heart attack before picking up a shovel, like chest pressure, shortness of breath, nausea and radiating arm pain. Stop immediately if you experience these symptoms and seek medical help. “Hire someone else to shovel, especially if you are at a high cardiac risk,” Serwer says.

Dress in layers and cover exposed skin in freezing temperatures and wind. Even with these efforts, frostbite and hypothermia are real risks. Frostbite begins in extremities like fingers and toes, and exposed facial skin. Early signs include pale, cold skin and prickling or numb sensations. Hypothermia happens when core body temperatures drop too low and begins with clumsiness, foggy thinking, fatigue and intense shivering. Stop immediately and go inside to warm up if you experience these symptoms.

“It is very easy to become dehydrated while working in cold climates,” Serwer says, as the human body suppresses the thirst response and dry winter air pulls additional moisture from our bodies. Notice signs of dehydration like fatigue, dry throat, cracked lips or a headache. “Dehydration is often overlooked, and people don’t replace the fluids as needed,” Serwer adds. Stop and take regular water breaks and continue drinking fluids for the remainder of the day if you notice these signs.

Shoveling puts strain on your spine and back, and can lead to serious, long term injuries like herniated disks, sciatica and lower back strains if you’re not careful. Beyond always lifting with your legs, stop shoveling if you feel the early signs of spine and back strain. These include a dull, aching in your lower back, sharp pain when bending or twisting, muscle cramping or shooting pains.

It is safer to push snow rather than lift it.

Individuals with heart disease, obesity, diabetes and high blood pressure should not shovel snow. Those over 45 years old should also exercise caution.

Before we began testing, we researched more than three dozen products, ranging from small portable options to professional-style equipment and even a few steam carpet cleaners. We considered weight, cord length, and accessories, and we also looked at carpet cleaner reviews to determine what made potential picks exceptional.

We then tested 23 different carpet cleaners on a carpet swatch marked by several tough-to-clean stains, including red wine, chocolate, dirt, and oil. We also used them around the house on old stains and furniture when possible, trying all included accessories, carrying each machine up and down stairs, and monitoring how long the carpet took to dry after use. We then rated each machine on how quickly and how well it eliminated stains, overall ease of use, portability, and suction, and assigned our favorite models awards based on their strengths.

Carpet cleaning equipment often features various cleaning modes and includes several accessories. Hose and cord length affect how long the unit can continuously clean before unplugging and moving. Keeping these factors in mind when shopping can help ensure you pick the best residential carpet cleaner for your needs.

Spot-cleaning machines are lightweight, portable, and less expensive than whole-house cleaners, but their suction isn’t as strong as larger units. A handheld carpet cleaner is ideal for use on stairs, in homes with just a couple of carpeted rooms, or on area rugs. These small carpet cleaners are also good for cleaning the carpets in the car.

Whole-house or upright carpet cleaners have robust motors, powerful suction, and thick, rotating brushes that provide deep cleaning. Many models offer multiple cleaning modes and use their own cleaning solutions, making them better suited to larger homes with many carpeted rooms that see heavy traffic. A whole-house, heavy-duty carpet cleaner is ideal for lifting dirt and grime that’s settled deep into carpet or rug fibers.

Buyers will want to consider their physical limits, the amount of carpeting, and the number of levels in the home when making a decision. In general, the heavier the machine, the more powerful its suction motor and rotating brushes will be. Portable carpet cleaners, like handheld carpet cleaners, are lighter and easier to maneuver, whereas full-size upright machines capable of heavy-duty cleaning will be harder to move and store.

Cord and hose length both affect cleaning time; the less often you have to unplug and plug in, the more efficient the cleaning session. Long cords of 20 feet or more and hoses up to 10 feet are particularly helpful in large rooms and for cleaning stairs. Since some upright units don’t have hoses, buyers wanting to clean under heavy pieces of furniture will want to be careful when choosing.

Carpet-cleaner accessories are attachments that can be added to a hose or intake port for cleaning different materials, reaching difficult areas, or dealing with pet hair and odors. Some of the most common types include upholstery cleaners; crevice-cleaning attachments (handy for tight spots like the indent created where the baseboard meets the carpet); or spinning brushes that lift tough, stuck-on stains. Pet attachments include special brushes, guards, and even isolated tanks for trapping fur to prevent it from getting caught in the machine. Many machines include samples of the brand’s best carpet shampoos or cleaning solutions to help you start cleaning right away.

Before buying or renting a carpet cleaner to keep your carpet looking new, take a look at these frequently asked questions and their answers.

The price range in this lineup is $125 to $700. However, the average cost of hiring a professional carpet cleaner is about $50 per room and can be up to $600 for larger homes. This means that after just a few uses, your new carpet cleaner will have paid for itself. You also have the option of renting carpet-cleaning equipment and DIYing the job at an average price of $30 per day. Either of these routes may make sense if you have just one or two carpeted rooms, but if your entire house is carpeted or you live with small children or furry friends, it may be more cost-effective to compare carpet cleaners and invest in your own unit.

If regular vacuuming and moderate care are taken, a carpet can be cleaned once every 12 to 18 months. In an active household with pets and children, you’ll want to clean the carpet every 6 to 12 months.

The best carpet cleaner for pets can remove pet hair, odors, and stains from even the deepest fibers of the carpet. In our tests, the Shark CarpetXpert HairPro Pet With StainStriker did a great job on these tasks as well as on more serious pet messes.

Bissell recommends staying off carpet for 4 to 6 hours after cleaning, but total dry time depends on a variety of factors, including the type of carpet fibers, the pile, how much solution and water were used, room size, ventilation, humidity, and temperature. Carpet made from polyester takes between 6 and 12 hours to dry, but wool carpet takes at least 24 hours to dry. To reduce drying time, use a quick-cleaning mode, which releases less liquid, and increase ventilation by opening windows, turning on fans, and turning on heat or air conditioning.

If you want to remove surface stains or odors, shampooing your carpets will be better. To deep clean and sanitize carpet, a steam cleaner will be more effective.

How much you should spend on a carpet cleaner depends on your needs regarding features, size, and frequency of use. The carpet cleaners selected for this guide cost between $125 and $700, which reflects the typical price range for reliable models.
