During our week of testing, we programmed this smart thermostat to follow a 7-day schedule, which we could do either directly on the display or through the intuitive and easy-to-use app. We could also select an optional energy-saving mode to reduce electricity costs.

The Honeywell thermostat syncs with digital assistants, including Google Home and Amazon Alexa. A C-wire and a home Wi-Fi network are required to operate the thermostat.

We liked the tabs on the touch screen that made it easy to access various settings, set schedules, and even view a weather forecast all with the touch of a finger. You can even change the color scheme on the thermostat.

While we liked this Honeywell smart thermostat, we were disappointed that it lacked key features that are common on most smart thermostats at this price point, namely geofencing functionality and a vacation mode.

Get the Honeywell Home Wi-Fi 9000 home thermostat at Amazon.

The Ecobee Premium Smart Thermostat claims that it will take keeping your home at the optimal temperature to the next level. We did like the interface and app. However, the Ecobee failed to deliver on the extras that are supposed to separate it from more affordable smart thermostats. We were most excited about the sensor that provides air quality reports. However, the thermostat was attempting to calibrate the air quality sensor during the entire testing period—a process that the manual notes should only take 24 hours. More importantly, our testing revealed significant issues with controlling gas furnace temperature: The Ecobee routinely heated the room to 3 to 4 degrees Fahrenheit above the set temperature before finally cutting it off (we verified the actual room temperature through the use of two independent room thermometers). Given these problems and the steep price tag, we’d be hard-pressed to recommend this model.

We looked at 30 different home thermostats to narrow our choices down to the top models on our list. Our selections come from some of the best-known brands in thermostats and cover a broad range of price points, from basic digital models to premium smart thermostats.

We assessed each home thermostat by installing and using each one for about a week. During that testing period, we assessed how well they performed their basic function of controlling a home’s heating, ventilation, and air conditioning (HVAC) system and maintaining set temperatures. We also used and evaluated any additional features, including schedule programming and, if applicable, smart features like geofencing, auto-scheduling, smartphone apps, and any smart sensors included with the thermostat.

While you might be tempted to run out and buy a smart thermostat that promises energy efficiency, don’t pull out the credit card until you’re sure it’s the right pick for your home. The best home thermostats are compatible with an existing heating and cooling system, offer features to make life simpler, and fit within your budget, which includes allowing for professional installation costs if necessary.

When it comes to choosing the best home thermostat, one size does not fit all. Some thermostats only control heat; some only control cooling, and some control both. The type of thermostat required depends on the HVAC system in the home. To determine the type of thermostat their home needs, shoppers will want to remember:

Smart thermostats may require users to place sensors in various rooms around the home to sense activity, monitor the temperature, and adjust the heating and cooling accordingly. While they add to a thermostat’s expense, Morey says they’re worth it. “Many of the latest smart thermostats offer remote temperature and humidity sensors that can be placed throughout the home,” he explains. “The thermostat can wirelessly connect to these sensors and control the temperature in a home in a way that keeps your comfort consistent throughout the home.” When any of these factors change or deviate from the norm, the sensor will trigger the thermostat to send an alert to the user’s smartphone.

The best home thermostat is easy to see and program. These days, many manual and programmable thermostats feature large LED screen displays and easy-to-follow prompts. These prompts help the user set the room temperature and program a custom heating and cooling schedule directly through the thermostat.

While you can set some smart thermostats much the same way as the manual and programmable varieties, their programming capabilities can be a bit more limited. Many smart thermostats are built with a small screen and require you to program them via an app that you must download and access through a smartphone, tablet, or PC.

Replacing an existing manual or programmable thermostat with a new manual or programmable model is relatively simple: The existing wires simply connect to the new thermostat. Installing this type of thermostat is often a DIY project.

Replacing an existing smart thermostat with a new one may also be a DIY project. However, if a C-wire is not available, running a new one is typically a job for an electrician. Installing the smart thermostat is only the first part of the task. Next, the user must download an app and follow the prompts to connect the thermostat to the home’s Wi-Fi network. Most of the time, this is relatively simple with a basic knowledge of routers and networks.

Thermostats were always meant to be functional, not decorative. While many basic models that lean more toward functionality are still available today, a lot has changed over the years in terms of aesthetics. These days, many thermostats have sleek digital display screens that look more appealing than their older counterparts. Some allow users to download a chosen background image onto the display. Most are low profile, so they don’t stick out far from the wall. A few newer models are even designed for recessing in a wall stud space, making the front of the screen nearly flush with the wall’s surface for a sleek, clean look.

Before upgrading to a new thermostat, many shoppers often have questions about which option they should choose. While some would rather stick to a functional, manual thermostat, others interested in creating cooling and heating schedules want to know more about programmable and smart options. Here are a few of the most frequently asked questions and their answers about the latest thermostats.

Probably, but some additional wiring may be required to install a smart thermostat if the home is more than 5 to 10 years old.

A smart thermostat connects to your home’s Wi-Fi network to relay information and allows you to control the HVAC system remotely or by voice commands.

Yes. Smart thermostats must connect to the Wi-Fi in a home so they can communicate with a smartphone.

Programmable thermostats can be smart or nonsmart. Select one that can schedule at least 7 days of heating and cooling and lets you override the schedule by adjusting the temperature.

Yes, if your home already has a C-wire installed. If your home doesn’t have a C-wire, a professional must install one first.

The features that make the thermostat “smart” (like geofencing and smartphone app control) won’t work when the internet is out, but you can still control the thermostat manually.

Dual coffee makers, also known as two-in-one or two-way coffee makers, typically produce full carafes of coffee along with single servings of drip coffee, instant coffee, espresso, and tea. They’re the ideal appliances for households with a variety of coffee preferences.

While choosing the best dual coffee maker might seem like a simple decision, there are actually a number of considerations to weigh. We’ve tested some of the top dual coffee makers on the market and reviewed them here so you can choose the ideal machine to fulfill your daily coffee fix. Our top choice was the Cuisinart Coffee Center 4-in-1 Barista Bar, but there are plenty of options to suit your coffee brewing needs.Read on for reviews of the best coffee makers available today.

Bottom line: Explore the best dual coffee makers of 2026, offering options for every budget and preference, from versatile all-in-one models to specialized espresso machines.

These top picks take into account key shopping considerations for the best dual coffee maker in addition to overall quality and value. Read on to discover some of the top-rated options on the market in a variety of categories for delicious coffee every time.

The versatility of this multifunctional barista bar helped it earn our top spot. Cuisinart’s Coffee Center is a great option for those who enjoy a variety of brews, from morning coffee to a pick-me-up cappuccino or espresso in the afternoon. It comes equipped with a standard 12-cup coffee maker on one side and a single-service brewer on the other. There’s also a steam wand that froths milk for cappuccinos, lattes, and the like.

Not only does it boast two separate reservoirs, one for the standard coffee maker and one for barista-style beverages, it has the ability to steam milk for a latte while simultaneously brewing a full pot of coffee. The single-service side works with 6-ounce, 8-ounce, and 10-ounce capsules, which means it can take both Nespresso capsules and Keurig K-cups.

In testing, we found that the control knob design makes it easy to toggle through and select from different brewing options. But we did have one gripe: The steam wand extended a little low for our usage; we had to search for a glass small enough to fit underneath it so we could froth our milk.

Cleaning the Cuisinart is similar to other dual coffee makers. We liked that most of the removable parts are dishwasher-safe, eliminating the need to hand-wash. While we appreciated the clean feature on the control panel, we’re not sure it’s much different from pressing the “Brew” button. The Cuisinart is one of the larger dual-function coffee makers we tested. While it certainly offers space savings over a Nespresso or Keurig machine and coffee maker, it does take up a fair amount of real estate on the countertop. Still, that larger size is worth it given the versatility it offers.

What our tester says: “As for taste, the coffee-maker side produces robust flavors, especially when engaging the “Bold” option on the control panel. We tried both types of capsules in the single-serve side and found them to be comparable in flavor to the Nespresso and Keurig machines we tested.”—Tony Carrick, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the Cuisinart Coffee Center 4-in-1 dual coffee maker at Amazon or Wayfair.

Ninja’s specialty coffee maker is one of the most versatile products on the market, capable of brewing a full glass carafe of drip coffee as well as iced coffee and concentrated espresso-style drinks. The built-in milk frother allows you to heat milk and create silky foam for lattes, cappuccinos, and more.

Flavor and serving size options abound with this machine. Use the brew strength control feature to choose between three settings (classic brew, rich brew, super-rich brew) and then select from six brew sizes—single cup, XL single cup, travel mug, XL travel mug, half carafe, and full 10-cup carafe.

All these options could make setting up the Ninja confusing, especially when your brain is still trying to wake up. Luckily, Ninja makes the process easy thanks to a handy double-ended scoop that clearly labels the amount of grounds to add to the filter and a water reservoir with clear markings for each serving size option. The labeled control knob on the front of the unit makes it easy to dial in the desired size. There are also separate buttons for normal brewing, rich brew, iced coffee, and specialty 4-ounce espresso-style drinks. A built-in steaming wand folds out from the side of the machine for frothing milk.

We found that the Ninja makes a strong, good-tasting brew, especially when using the “Rich” setting. The frother is a nice addition but, unlike with some models we tested, milk must be frothed manually by holding a cup of milk under the wand. This requires a bit more effort to create a cappuccino, latte, or some other specialty drink.

Overall, the Ninja is an excellent and surprisingly affordable choice for anyone who wants to brew coffee as well as a variety of other types of coffee drinks.

With loads of Nespresso flavors to choose from (the Lattissima comes with a large sample pack), coffee fans have plenty of options when it comes to the strength and flavor of specialty drinks. Yet while we love how the Lattissima takes the effort out of brewing, the machine cannot brew more than one drink at a time, and it doesn’t make regular coffee. That said, given that the Lattissima is compact at just about 6 inches wide by 13 inches deep, it’s certainly possible to pair it with a traditional coffee machine on a kitchen counter.

This dual coffee maker brews a full 12-cup glass carafe on one side and single-serving pods on the other. Various aspects of this Cuisinart’s design impressed us in testing. We liked that each side has its own reservoir, so users needn’t empty and refill the reservoir when switching from one brewing mode to the other. We also liked the labeled buttons on the front of the machine that make it a breeze to choose between pods and/or carafe. There’s a control to adjust the temperature of the carafe, which is ideal for those who may not like steaming hot coffee.

In terms of taste, we appreciated the brew strength controls. We found that this machine made rich, flavorful coffee, especially when engaging the “Bold” button. There’s also a button for pausing the coffee maker, which is ideal for grabbing a quick cup mid-brew. For those who want a single serving from coffee grounds as opposed to K-cups, the Coffee Center includes a special single-serving coffee filter that fits into the K-cup holder. With its Extreme Brew feature, we also found that the Cuisinart brews a full carafe more quickly than other coffee makers.

This coffee maker also purports to create iced coffee with its “Over Ice” button, but unfortunately in testing it failed to work properly—the coffee still came out quite hot. Aside from this issue, we found the Cuisinart 2-in-1 coffee maker to be a great option for those who like to switch between K-cups and a full carafe.

Get the Cuisinart Coffee Center 2-in-1 coffee maker at Amazon or Best Buy.

We researched models from the top coffee maker brands and selected and tested those with high customer satisfaction. The selection process factored in brew capacity and sizes, functionality, and special features. Each coffee maker in our lineup comes with a carafe and produces a maximum of 10 or 12 cups of coffee.

Most of the top picks offer two or more brew strengths to accommodate different personal preferences. Select options have a built-in milk frother and accept K-cups or pods. The majority of the coffee makers on the list feature durable stainless steel components for longevity. Some models come with a charcoal filter that enhances flavor, 24-hour programmability, brew pausing, and auto shutoff.

Once assembled, we conducted side-by-side testing of each coffee maker. We considered how easy each machine was to set up, how quickly it brewed coffee, and, of course, the flavor of the finished product. Since these are dual coffee makers, we also tested all of their functions, including their ability to operate as a traditional coffee maker, brew cappuccinos and lattes, and brew with Nespresso cups and Keurig cups.

While it’s easy to assume that all dual coffee makers offer similar performance, several factors affect their functionality, including brew options, size, capacity, carafe type, programmable settings, availability of additional features, and more. Keep reading to learn about several of the most important features to consider when choosing the best dual coffee maker for your kitchen.

Dual coffee makers differ in the types of beverages they produce. Most brew a full carafe of coffee and single-serve coffee, boiling water for hot beverages, and espresso for crafting lattes and cappuccinos. Some models accept coffee pods, while others use ground coffee.

Grind-and-brew coffee makers provided added convenience for those who want freshly ground coffee. When choosing a dual coffee maker with a built-in grinder, look for a model that uses burrs rather than blades. Burrs produce a more consistent grind and generate less heat, so the flavor of the coffee isn’t diminished.

Consider the kitchen’s available countertop space and how much coffee each household member consumes daily. Given their multifunctionality, some dual coffee makers are quite large, taking up approximately 1 square foot of counter space.

Coffee-maker capacity is measured in cups. Keep in mind that “cup” measurements provided by coffee machine manufacturers don’t necessarily align with the standard unit of measurement. A standard U.S. cup measures 8 ounces, while a “cup” from a coffee maker may only measure 4 to 6 ounces.

Coffee makers usually feature either a glass or a thermal carafe, which use different methods to keep coffee warm.

Some dual coffee makers don’t feature a carafe at all, instead dispensing coffee directly into a mug.

Dual coffee makers generally have a variety of programmable settings.

Standard coffee makers typically feature several removable parts that must be cleaned regularly, including the carafe, filter basket, and reusable filter. Dual coffee makers tend to feature even more complex makeups due to their advanced functionality. Look for a model with minimal parts that you can easily assemble and disassemble for cleaning. Those prioritizing ease of cleaning will also want to consider dual coffee makers with dishwasher-safe parts.

Dual coffee makers offer a variety of additional features.

Not quite ready to start brewing? Check out the answers to some of the most frequently asked questions about dual coffee makers.

Dual brew coffee makers vary in their functionality. Most produce a full carafe of drip coffee as well as espresso; single-serve coffee; and boiling water for instant coffee, tea, and cocoa.

Some dual coffee makers, but not all, feature grinders.

Look for a coffee maker with a capacity that suits your household’s needs and brews the type of coffee you enjoy most.

#7711. Has That Final Destination Truck Scene Ever Actually Happened in Real Life?

Here's what real-world crash data actually says about the likelihood of a Final Destination truck scene.

Giving drivers a reason to fear logging trucks since 2003, Final Destination 2 opened with one of the franchise’s most visceral—and memorable—scenes. A logging truck traveling down a busy highway spills its cargo and sets off a chain reaction of intense car crashes. It’s a gruesome, cinematic disaster, but the basic danger is grounded in reality.  Logs can come loose during transport, with serious consequences on a busy road.  Has anything like the Final Destination truck scene actually happened in real life?

Yes, there have been real-life incidents where logging trucks lost their cargo and caused major highway accidents. However, the Final Destination truck scene depicting this realistic road hazard is grossly exaggerated. Logs can fall off of trucks and cause accidents, but they don’t bounce down the highway and become windshield-level projectiles like in the film. So, yes, the danger is real, but the chain-reaction chaos depicted in the film is highly dramatized.

In January 2024, a logging truck on Interstate 95 in Florida overturned while traveling too fast through a curve in the road. Logs spilled onto the highway, rolled over a barrier and into oncoming traffic. A Jacksonville man who was involved in the accident told local reporters, “I just had a real life Final Destination moment…” However, he and all other motorists were unharmed. In June of 2025, another turnover dumped not logs, but large metal pipes across Highway 75 in Tulsa, Oklahoma, closing both lanes of traffic. Again, no injuries were reported. A fatal accident involving a logging truck did occur in Arkansas in 2014. While traveling down Highway 65, the truck blew a rear tire, swerved into a bridge construction site and tipped over. Two construction workers were killed by the discharged logs.

Each year, shifting or unsecured loads carried by commercial vehicles are linked to roughly 4,000 to 7,000 accidents. This may not sound like a lot, but these accidents have severe consequences, often resulting in serious injury or death. “They regularly make news headlines, so the average person may think they’re more common than they are,” personal injury attorney Juan Dominguez says. In fact, the most dangerous vehicles carrying cargo are non-commercial cars and trucks. 73 percent of highway accidents involving road debris are caused by passenger vehicles with unsecured loads. Commercial trucks are closely regulated and inspected for proper load security, contributing to lower accident rates. Despite the attention given to logging truck accidents, they are only involved in 1.5 percent of all fatal commercial truck accidents each year.

Take control of your safety when sharing the road with large cargo trucks. Here’s how:

“My first rule is to never drive directly behind a truck with a [loose] load like logs, pipes or steel beams,” construction safety specialist Steven Menotti says. “If the load shifts or falls off, you’ll be the first vehicle it hits.” If you have to drive behind a cargo truck,  increase your following distance to at least four seconds, which allows for more reaction time if debris falls into the road. “That distance can help if the unexpected happens and something comes loose,” Dominguez says. “You have more time to try and react.” If possible, reduce your speed for a shorter stopping distance.

If you need to pass a truck on the highway, time it so you can quickly complete the pass and return to the lane. Avoid driving directly next to a cargo truck for an extended length of time to avoid being hit by falling debris or cargo.

If you spot a truck without a properly secured load, move away from it on the road. Look for worn or loose straps and chains, unevenly loaded cargo or missing side stakes. “Those all indicate the trucker probably didn’t check the load,” Menotti says. “I won’t follow it. I change lanes, and pull far back.”

Logs can fall from trucks, but they don’t bounce or become projectiles across the highway like the Final Destination truck scene. In the film, this depiction was CGI-generated.

Brake hard and avoid swerving. Swerving causes 37 percent of all road debris accident fatalities, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA).

Major U.S. law firms are giving associates raises and establishing a new market rate ranging from $235,000 for first-year lawyers to $455,000 for senior associates, plus additional bonuses. (Image from Shutterstock)

Major U.S. law firms are giving associates raises and establishing a new market rate ranging from $235,000 for first-year lawyers to $455,000 for senior associates, plus additional bonuses.

Cravath, Swaine & Moore’s associate salary scale was increased Tuesday, and it rivals the raises announced in June at Milbank, according to coverage by Reuters.

Milbank increased the associate salary range from $235,000 to $455,000. In July, it offered special bonuses between $6,000 and $25,000 for associates. Reuters is also reporting pay increases at Fried, Frank, Harris, Shriver & Jacobson and Cleary Gottlieb Steen & Hamilton.

Cravath’s special bonuses—$11,000 to $40,000—based on class year, exceeded Milbank’s scale. Its year-end bonus scale starts at $15,000 and extends to $115,000, which is a continuation of what the firm and others offered in past years.

#7707. Bob Woodward Interviews Justice Kagan, Or Does Justice Kagan Interview Bob Woodward

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Kagan sheds some light on her view about leaks, Dobbs, and the Court.

Last month I wrote about an excerpt from Bob Woodward's new book that reveals sources. Most of the sources are deceased, so there is little harm outing them. But Justices Kagan and Breyer are alive and well. Woodward reveals a remarkable conversation with the former. As Woodward would observe, it is less clear that he was interviewing Kagan than Kagan was interviewing him.

"Well, the conclusion of The Brethren was that the center of the court was in control," I said, meaning neither the left nor the right was in charge. "Yes, I prefer it that way," Kagan said. "That's exactly what it should be." That's not the way it is now, I noted. It is not, Kagan confirmed. How did you get such detail in the book? We had time, I said. Of course, it was a different era in which Scott and I were doing the reporting in the late 1970s. I started to tell her about Scott and how he had really discovered the Nixon Tapes because he found Alexander Butterfield. Not letting me off the hook, Kagan asked again, "How did you do it?" Well, we interviewed five sitting justices and 170 law clerks. We got documentation. That's extraordinary, Kagan said. How did you get the documents? The justices must have approved the clerks giving you the documents? I shook my head. Not that we were aware. You make clerks now sign nondisclosure agreements, I noted. "Yes," she said.

Over the years, I've speculated that Justices have authorized their clerks to leak information to the press. The premise of Kagan's questions is that Justices had authorized their clerks to speak with Woodward and Bernstein. But no, the clerks went rogue. If the clerks acted alone in the 1970s, perhaps they did so in 2022 with the Dobbs opinion.

I told her that Brennan and Marshall, the liberal justices on the court, would not help us. Well, who did? Rehnquist and White, I said. Kagan seemed surprised. I recounted the story of calling Justice Lewis Powell at the court one morning and him agreeing to meet. I said when and he said now. "I was in my pajamas, but told him I'd be there in half an hour." You must be fast, Kagan said. I was then, I joked. I was 79 now and slow.

Justice Kagan clerked for Justice Marshall, who apparently never discussed the sourcing for The Brethren.

Is all of this known about The Brethren? Kagan asked. I didn't have an answer so instead I dived into Blackmun's role in Roe v. Wade and how he had drafted the opinion at the Mayo Clinic library. "I thought the leak of the Dobbs decision was a public service," I told her, referencing the decision that had overturned Roe the previous year. I can't say I agree with that, Kagan said. Why do you think it's a public service? Well, the court took away a right that had been there for 50 years. The public needed to know so there could be a debate. Kagan didn't say anything.

I find it odd that Kagan said nothing in response. This is not the sort of statement that could trigger a recusal. She might have said "that debate nearly got my colleague assassinated." But she stayed silent.

I said from reporting more than 50 years on 10 presidents, I thought there was such a concentration of power in the presidency. Too much power.

She nodded. It's why Trump was able to get away with so much, I said. Kagan did not respond. Then I said, there's too much power in the Supreme Court maybe. She noticeably reacted to that, her head held a little higher, her posture stiffening. Her only reply was, "That's interesting."

She mustered a response here, but not to the leak question. Interesting?

"Are you happy on the court?" I asked her. No, I'm not, given the situation, Kagan replied. I was surprised at her candor.

Kagan likely didn't think she would be quoted.

As we parted ways, she smiled warmly and said she respected my work and I said I respected hers. Late that night I recorded a detailed voice memo of my conversation with Kagan for my assistant to transcribe. It is hard to tell who was interviewing who.

On Saturday, October 21, 2023, Elsa and I attended a dinner for the 50th anniversary of the Saturday Night Massacre hosted by the former Watergate special prosecutors at the WilmerHale law firm in downtown Washington. The main speaker was retired Supreme Court justice Stephen Breyer, who had been a junior Watergate prosecutor. Elsa sat next to Breyer at the dinner before switching seats with me. He had served 28 years on the Supreme Court and told her he was "forced out" so someone younger could take his place.

No one forced him out. He has life tenure. Instead, Breyer surrendered to the pressure. So much for judicial independence. Justices Alito and Thomas are often charged with being MAGA partisans, but they exhibited robust independence from political forces.

Woodward offers this anecdote about the Thomas confirmation hearing:

Later Gray told me it took five years for Clarence Thomas to recover. Justice Thomas's wife, Ginni Thomas, a conservative activist, approached me at a conference in Washington one day. She said after the hearings her husband was never really a whole person again. He hardened. Many conservatives, including attorney general for George H. W. Bush and for Donald Trump, Bill Barr, have said the hearings pushed Thomas to the hard right.

I couldn't find any references to other current justices.

I will read the chapters on The Brethren with interest.

Josh Blackman is a constitutional law professor at the South Texas College of Law Houston and the President of the Harlan Institute. Follow him @JoshMBlackman.

#7706. This DIY Coffee Station Can Be Built Using Only Scrap Wood

Give your coffee maker a home with this coffee station organizer.

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

Clear the counter clutter and fuel your mornings with a scrap-wood coffee station that has a spot for everything.

If you know three things about me, it’s that I’m a stickler for organization, I run on coffee, and I can’t throw away wood scraps. This coffee station checks all three boxes.

It’s built almost entirely from maple offcuts, which explains the mix of thicknesses on the Cutting List. To keep it approachable, every joint is a simple butt joint with glue and brad nails. Biscuits are used only for the glued-up panels. If you can make square cuts and run a nailer, you can build this in a weekend.

[Please insert TA “Coffee_org_case.pdf” here with callouts.]

[Please insert TA “Coffee_org_drawer.pdf” here with callouts.]

Boards wide enough for the top (A) and base (B) are almost impossible to find, so I made the panels by joining several boards with biscuits.

Cut the boards at least 1/2-in. longer and wider than needed. The extra material lets you trim the panels square and to size after the glue dries.

Mark across each joint where you want a biscuit, spacing them 6- to 8-in. apart and about 3-in. from each end. Cut the slots with a biscuit joiner. Be generous with the glue in the slots and along the edges. You want an even bead of squeeze-out so you know you have good coverage. Clamp the panels and keep them flat as they dry.

Once the glue dries, scrape off the squeeze-out and cut the top (A) and base (B) to the final size. Then cut the rest of the parts following the cutting list.

Connect the two sides (C) and the back (E) to the base (B) of the coffee organizer using 18-gauge brad nails and wood glue. Secure the sides so they’re flush with the bottom of the base. Set the back on the base between the sides, flush with the back edges of the base (B) and sides (C).

Cut the pieces for the butcher block (L) and biscuit-join them the same way you did the panels. Again, cut them at least 1/2-in. oversize. That allows for the wood shifting during clamping and leaves enough on each end to make clean, square cuts once the glue has dried.

Once the glue is dry, cut the butcher block to final size on the table saw. Scrape and sand off the dried glue, then round over the sharp edges with a router and a bearing-guided 1/4-in. round-over bit.

When you size the butcher block, leave room for the drawer slides you’ll install later. Most need about 1/2-in. on each side, so a 13-in. opening takes a 12-in.-wide butcher block.

The left-hand compartment houses the butcher block and drawer, so it needs to be 13-in. wide: 12-in. for the butcher block and drawer, plus 1-in. for the drawer slides. Mark the divider location, then test-fit the butcher block and loose drawer slides to confirm the opening. Apply glue and secure the center divider (D) with 18-gauge brad nails driven up through the base (B) and in through the back (E).

Note: Drawer slide clearance varies by style and manufacturer. Check your slides’ specs and adjust the opening as needed.

Build a drawer to store coffee pods and spoons. Glue and nail the drawer box front and back (G) to the ends of the sides (F), then attach the bottom (H) to square it up. The drawer front (K) covers the nails on the front.

Secure the drawer dividers (J) inside the drawer (Fig. B) with wood glue and brad nails, spacing them to fit your coffee pods, spoons, or other items. Feel free to add or take away dividers as needed. I left 1-1/2-in.-wide slots for pods and a 4-in.-wide slot for spoons.

On the left side of the coffee organizer, install the butcher block (L) and drawer using your drawer slides and the included hardware. Both attach to the left side (C) and center divider (D), so install the butcher block first and the drawer above it. Pre-drill and hand-screw for proper alignment and to avoid stripping the screws.

Once the butcher block (L) and drawer are installed, cover the left compartment with the top (A), securing it with glue and 18-gauge brad nails. The right side stays open.

Then attach the drawer front (K) to the drawer box front so it overlaps the left side (C) and center divider (D). Use double-sided tape to position it and 1-in. screws from inside the drawer box to lock it down.

Install and secure dividers on the right side of the unit with 1-1/4-inch 18-gauge brad nails and wood glue. Working from the front to the back of the coffee station:

In the 6-1/4-in. space between the front face (M) and the short divider (N), install the tea separators (R) and spacers (S and T) to make a divided area for sugar, teas, stirrers, etc. Use a 23-gauge nailer and 5/8-in. nails to secure the spacers (S and T) to the front face (M) and short divider (N), then slide the tea separators (R) into the gaps between them. My compartments were 2-1/8-in. and 3-in. wide, but feel free to make them whatever size you’d like.

Sink any protruding nails, fill the nail holes with wood filler, and finish-sand the entire piece. Apply a finish to the whole unit. I used Tried & True Original Wood Finish, which is food-safe, so it works on the butcher block and everything else

Then install the handles on the drawer and butcher block. You can’t reach behind the solid butcher block to drive a screw, so cut the head off the handle screw with a hacksaw, drill a pilot hole, and glue the cut end into it with CA glue or epoxy.

A food-safe wood finish won’t transfer chemicals or toxins to the food when being used. There are two ways a finish is considered food-safe. Either it is completely non-toxic and edible in its liquid state from its origin, or, once fully cured, the VOCs (volatile organic compounds) in the finish disperse, and it becomes a stable, inert, non-toxic solid. Finishes like food-grade mineral oil or fractionated coconut oil are considered food-safe from the time of application and work well as food-safe wood finishes.

A coffee station should include options for coffee or tea, sweeteners, flavoring and stirring. Focus on organization and easy access tiers – no matter what you choose to present in your coffee station.

42-in. works well for a free-standing coffee station cabinet. This is slightly higher than a standard 36-in. countertop height and lower than a 45-in. bar height top. For a coffee station on a countertop beneath upper cabinets, you want enough clearance to open and close your coffee maker’s lid. A 6-in. tall coffee station would give you 12-in. clearance in a standard 18-in. opening between the top of the counter and the bottom of the upper cabinets.

#7705. The Best Countertop Water Filters of 2026, Tested for Chlorine, Heavy Metals, and More

Black Friday Deals Are Already Here ➡️ Tools, Generators, Essentials & More

By Michelle Larson, Additional research provided by Alisa Martin

Published Nov 24, 2026 10:00 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Staying properly hydrated has many health benefits—it promotes cardiovascular health, enhances skin elasticity, and eliminates waste from the body—and using a countertop water filter is an easy way to get safe, clean drinking water right in your kitchen. These user-friendly appliances either sit on your counter or attach to your faucet, removing common contaminants like chemicals, heavy metals, and bacteria without requiring permanent plumbing. Not only that, they help reduce the plastic waste associated with buying bottled water.

To help you find the right one for your water quality and household needs, we spent 2 weeks testing seven of the most popular models on the market today. Based on our results, we chose the Bluevua Countertop Reverse Osmosis Water Filter System as our favorite for its easy setup, third-party contaminant removal certifications, long filter life, and remineralization stage that restores beneficial minerals for a smooth taste. Read on for our detailed reviews of the best countertop water filters and to learn what matters most when choosing the one for you.

Bottom line: Countertop water filters offer a convenient way to access clean, safe drinking water, with options to suit various needs and budgets.

The products below represent the “best in show” in home water filtration. These top picks were chosen based on quality, functionality, and reputation.

This was the first unit we tested, and it ended up being our favorite. Installation was incredibly easy—just fill the removable water reservoir, plug the unit in, and press start. As with any reverse osmosis (RO) water filter system, you’ll also want to discard the first two tanks of water as part of flushing the new filters, but after that, you’ll get nothing but pure, great-tasting water. In fact, we thought the water from this model was some of the best, due to its comprehensive filtration as well as the fact that it undergoes a remineralization stage to add calcium and magnesium back in for a super smooth taste.

Another favorite feature was the built-in LCD screen that shows total dissolved solids (TDS) before and after each cycle, giving us visible proof that its NSF- and WQA-certified filtration system was actively removing contaminants. That display also shows when it’s time to replace each of the four filters (they all have relatively long lifespans of 12 to 24 months), and changing them is easy since they twist right out (there’s also a reset button for each one to update its filter life indicator). We also really liked that it dispenses directly into a glass carafe that maintains the water’s crisp taste and fits easily into our fridge. The Bluevua isn’t the least expensive model on this list, but for an RO unit with remineralization, it provides an excellent value—provided you have the counter space for it.

What our tester says: “I’ve been drinking alkaline water for years, and I greatly prefer it to the flat taste of reverse osmosis water. Since the Bluevua gives me both, it’s my new favorite water filter!”—Michelle Larson, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the Bluevua countertop water filter at Amazon or Bluevua.

As another RO system with remineralization, this Waterdrop gave the Bluevua a real run for its money. We loved the slightly lower price point and slightly smaller footprint, but it ultimately came in second because it (unlike several others in the brand’s lineup) is yet to hold any third-party certifications—though we hope it’s just a matter of time since this model is relatively new. Like the Bluevua, it features a digital display that shows TDS levels before and after filtration, and like every unit we tested, it passed our manual water-quality tests with flying colors.

While traditional RO systems can be a bit of a pain to install, setting up this countertop reverse osmosis filter is as easy as plugging it in, filling the reservoir, and throwing away the first couple of pitchers. You can filter water directly into your own container or the included 32-ounce water tank, which means you can chill one batch in the fridge while still having the option to grab a quick room-temp cup. And since the seven-stage filtration process takes place inside a single composite cartridge, maintenance is incredibly easy even if it’s a little more frequent (there’s a filter life indicator, and Waterdrop says to expect replacement about every 12 months). Considering its budget-friendly price point, sleek design, and delicious water, there are days we might actually vote this model number one.

What our tester says: “I’ve actually tested a couple of Waterdrop water filters now, and each has been a pleasure to use. The company consistently prioritizes user-friendliness, and because this RO model also adds minerals back in, the final product tastes excellent.”—Michelle Larson, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the Waterdrop countertop water filter at Amazon or Waterdrop.

If you want reliable multi-stage water filtration without giving up counter space or worrying about cords, this simple pitcher filter from Epic could be ideal. The simple gravity-fed setup is compact enough for small apartments and dorm rooms and user-friendly enough for anyone seeking straightforward pour-in, pour-out convenience. Despite its small footprint, it offers as much or more capacity than many options on this list, storing easily on the counter or in the fridge.

In terms of technology, the Pure XP uses a nanofiber and carbon-block core to reduce over 70 common drinking water contaminants—including heavy metals, forever chemicals (PFAS), microplastics, and parasites—while retaining naturally occurring trace minerals. It holds an array of third-party certifications and uses BPA- and BPS-free materials to avoid introducing any chemicals back in. Cleaning and maintenance are easy: simply hand wash the pitcher and swap out the inner cartridge every 3 to 4 months (the outer portion is reusable to cut down on plastic waste). This means you may end up spending a little more on replacement filters than you would with some other systems, but given the very reasonable purchase price, you’re definitely still getting a good deal.

What our tester says: “If you’re looking for a classic Brita-style pitcher but want to be sure it’s pulling out all the gunk you don’t want, this is it. It’s also incredibly easy to use, and the water tastes great!”—Michelle Larson, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the Epic Water Filters countertop water filter at Amazon or Epic Water Filters.

Setting up the Waterdrop M6CG couldn’t have been much easier. After filling the rear reservoir and getting everything running, we were impressed by how neatly the unit fit into a coffee and tea station despite giving you both hot and cold filtered water. We initially wished there was an option to connect it directly to a water line, but since an RO system also needs somewhere to send wastewater, the refillable tank setup will probably be more practical for most kitchens anyway. Most importantly, the filtered water tasted noticeably better than our unfiltered tap water, and the hot-water function gave us water that was more than hot enough for tea without waiting for a kettle.

Our biggest complaint is dispensing speed. Compared with a refrigerator dispenser or traditional water cooler, the Waterdrop feels extremely slow, particularly when filling a mug with hot water. The touchscreen is attractive and generally intuitive, but things get more cumbersome when you want a quantity that isn’t one of the presets. Dialing in our preferred 10-ounce serving took more tapping than expected, though thankfully the machine lets you save custom settings as favorites.

We also liked the glass carafe attached to the machine, which fills from the bottom and keeps room-temperature filtered water ready to grab at any time (it also looks and feels super premium). The system provides helpful reminders when the reservoir needs attention, although they can occasionally feel unnecessary, such as reminding us to refill or empty the tank while we’re already removing it to do exactly that. Overall, this is a capable, attractive RO dispenser that produces great-tasting water and useful hot and cold options. We just wish its dispensing speed and interface felt a little more polished given the premium price.

Get the Waterdrop M6CG countertop water filter at Amazon, Target, Best Buy, or Walmart.

Comparing the certifications of all the filtered water systems in this guide had its confusing moments, but as we worked, we learned that the AquaTru Classic RO system is one of the most highly certified units on the market. With its comprehensive four-stage design, it can trap a total of 84 contaminants, including everything from coarse sediment and chlorine to heavy metals, fluoride, microplastics, and forever chemicals (PFAS). And with a 2.84-liter clean water tank, it also holds more purified water than any other reverse osmosis system on our list.

Because the filters last anywhere from 6 months to 2 years (depending on which of the three filters you’re replacing), maintenance is also minimal, especially compared to standard pitcher filters. Like all RO systems, though, it also takes up more counter space than basic units. Ultimately, its higher upfront cost and lack of remineralization kept it out of the top spot, but those with high-capacity demands who love everything else about it will be happy to hear AquaTru sells replacement filters with minerals—making cost the only real hurdle.

Get the AquaTru countertop water filter at Amazon, The Home Depot, Best Buy, or AquaTru.

One of the biggest downsides of faucet-connected systems is that their hoses can easily get in the way of other sink-related tasks, like washing your hands or doing the dishes. They also create a cluttered look, which Brondell seems to acknowledge, as the brand doesn’t show any photos of this model actually hooked up to a faucet. However, if you purchase an inexpensive T-valve and don’t mind drilling a small hole in your countertop, you can run that hose under your sink for a totally seamless look. And because this pick allows for virtually instant filtration, you get purified water on demand no matter which setup you choose.

Performance-wise, the Cypress countertop filter uses a three-stage system that combines a sediment filter, a patented Nanotrap filter, and a carbon block to pull out chlorine, microplastics, VOCs, and fine particles. Water dispenses instantly at the press of a button with zero wastewater generated, making it faster than gravity pitchers and more efficient than reverse osmosis setups. It also has a slim footprint that takes up minimal countertop space, though because it’s only about 10 inches tall, it’s hard to fill tall bottles or large pots (we had to reposition it over the sink to do so during testing). Still, it comes at a great price for a WQA Gold Seal-certified unit with filters that last 6 months to 1 year, making it a good water filter for homes with high-volume needs.

Get the Brondell countertop water filter at Amazon or Brondell.

There’s no denying the popularity of the Big Berkey: its stainless steel construction and massive 8.5-liter capacity have made it a staple for large households and off-grid enthusiasts. Because it relies strictly on gravity and its proprietary Black Berkey filters, it functions entirely without electricity, plumbing, or tap pressure—you simply pour water into the top chamber and let it drip down. It also has an extremely long filter lifespan of up to 6,000 gallons per pair, meaning you won’t be constantly buying replacements.

However, its popularity comes with a couple of drawbacks. Despite the hefty price tag, Berkey lacks any official certifications, relying instead on independent lab testing. And like all gravity systems, it’s also quite bulky, standing almost 20 inches tall with no option for fridge storage. Also, because it relies on gravity, the filtration rate is quite slow—we got into the habit of filling the top reservoir a couple of times a day so it had several hours to make its way to the bottom. Still, with no gauge of any sort, we never really had any idea how much water was even in the bottom chamber. All that aside, Berkey has an almost cult-like following, and the durable stainless steel water filter body and straightforward operation are likely why.

Get the Big Berkey countertop water filter at Amazon.

To find a selection of the best countertop water filters for home use, we began by evaluating dozens of popular models, focusing on ease of installation and use, filtration claims, capacity, and price.

After selecting seven units for testing, we performed the same set of steps with each, starting with installation. Next, we performed water quality tests before and after filtration to measure contaminant reduction, followed by blind taste tests to rate flavor and odor. We measured flow rate by timing how long each unit took to process or dispense a quart of water, assessed how easy each unit was to clean and change filters on, and rated general convenience of extra features like filter life indicators and removable pitchers.

We used each model for a minimum of 2 days to get a feel for how much we liked them overall, and for the faucet-connected models, to see whether they got in the way during regular tasks like washing hands or dishes.

The best countertop water filtration system for your home will depend on the quality concerns you want to address, how much filtered water your household uses, and how much daily upkeep you’re willing to take on. It’s smart to request a copy of your local utility’s Consumer Confidence Report or use a home water test kit, then compare potential systems’ filtration claims, capacity, footprint, and replacement-filter cost.

Countertop water filters generally fall into two broad categories: reservoir-based systems and faucet-connected systems. Reservoir models don’t connect to your plumbing at all, while faucet-connected models attach to a standard faucet or use a diverter valve under your sink.

Reservoir systems hold untreated water in one tank or chamber and deliver clean water into another after it passes through the system’s filter(s). The simplest versions are water pitchers like the Epic Water Filters Pure XP Water Filter Pitcher or gravity systems like the Big Berkey Gravity-Fed Water Filter. Since they don’t connect to your faucet, they’re great for apartments, dorms, RVs, and kitchens with incompatible faucets.

Countertop reverse osmosis systems also use a refillable reservoir, but rather than relying on gravity, they have an internal pump that forces the water through their filters before delivering it to a pitcher or your glass. RO systems have the added benefit of reducing dissolved solids in untreated water, but that includes beneficial minerals like calcium and magnesium and also creates wastewater that must be dumped (or used for things like cleaning or watering plants).

Faucet-connected filters either attach directly to your faucet or connect via a hose and diverter valve. When the diverter is switched to the filtration setting, tap water filters through the unit on demand and into your glass, bottle, or pot. When the diverter is off, water flows straight out of the tap as normal.

Two major things to consider regarding faucet-connected systems are faucet compatibility and installation. Most aren’t compatible with pull-down, pull-out, spray, sensor-operated, or nonstandard faucets, and many also have small hoses that connect the faucet to the machine, which takes up a bit of space and can look cluttered. Some allow you to run the hoses from the machine to the plumbing under your sink, but that will require an adapter and a hole in the counter for the cords to route through.

While it can be tempting to choose the purification system for water that has the longest list of contaminants removed, it’s ultimately more important to pair the system you choose with what you’re actually trying to filter out of your water.

Most of the best water filters have activated-carbon filters that remove unpleasant tastes and odors and may reduce other chemicals or particulates. Some systems add sediment filtration or specialty media to target things like lead, fluoride, or PFAS compounds. Since performance varies by model, always check the manufacturer’s claims rather than assuming they all work the same.

Reverse-osmosis systems use a membrane designed to reduce dissolved solids, which means they generally remove more contaminants than basic filtration systems. However, they can also reduce beneficial minerals, which is why some manufacturers are now adding a remineralization stage to return the filtered water to a more alkaline state.

Many of the units on this list carry third-party certification to verify tested performance beyond manufacturer claims. NSF International’s drinking-water treatment standards are the most commonly used, although you may also see mentions of accredited organizations like IAPMO R&T or WQA. While our tests using the Varify Complete Drinking Water Test Kit for this guide backed up the manufacturers’ claims, it’s still a good idea to prioritize products that carry filter certifications and look up which contaminants the product is certified to remove.

Then, match the certification to your specific concern. For example, if lead reduction is your main goal, you’ll want a model with NSF 53 and 58 listings.

Capacity has two meanings: how much water a filter can treat before replacement and how much filtered water the unit can provide at once. For our purposes, we’re defining it as how much it can filter at once, as we discuss filter life in the next section.

Since reservoir models’ ready-to-drink supply is based on the size of their clean-water chambers, larger households or those with greater needs will want to prioritize a model that holds multiple liters or gallons. Faucet-connected models can also be a good choice in those situations, as they can deliver clean water continuously as long as the tap is on.

Flow rate—how quickly the filter provides clean drinking water—is another important consideration. However, many manufacturers don’t list this information, and it can also vary depending on water pressure, source-water quality, temperature, and cartridge age. If this is a major concern, you may want to reach out to manufacturers directly or read online reviews for mentions of filtration speed.

Every countertop drinking water filter system requires filter replacement on a set schedule, which means the true cost of ownership ends up being more than what you paid for it. When choosing between systems, compare the number of filters, their individual projected filter capacity, and each one’s replacement cost.

A basic pitcher may use a single cartridge that’s easy to change but needs more frequent replacement, while a multistage RO unit may have multiple filters that each have different change intervals and prices. While systems with filter-life indicators can make it much easier to know when it’s time to swap them, if your unit is noticeably slower or isn’t providing the same quality, you may still need to change filters even if it isn’t technically time.

Countertop water filters are generally pretty straightforward, but the following answers to commonly asked questions can answer any lingering queries you may have.

Water filters work by using a filtration mechanism to capture organisms and chemicals that lead to unsafe or cloudy water. A fabricated surface traps the larger contaminants, while a compound like activated carbon works as a magnet to trap smaller contaminants.

Installation depends on the type: A faucet-connected filtration system typically attaches to a compatible faucet aerator or diverter valve, while dispenser, pitcher, gravity-fed, and countertop RO models generally only require rinsing the parts, installing the filters, and filling the reservoir. Always follow the manufacturer’s instructions, especially for RO units that may also require an initial flush cycle.

No, countertop water purification filters do not work with every type of kitchen faucet. Specifically, more modern designs and detachable faucets with spray nozzles may be incompatible with faucet-connected countertop water filters.

Most filters can remove chlorine, fluoride, bacteria, and parasites. To know exactly which contaminants a specific filter can remove or reduce, consult the manufacturer’s information regarding filter certification.

Yes, bacteria can grow in a countertop filter, so it’s a good idea to flush the faucet for about 20 seconds after turning on the water and then for an additional 5 to 10 seconds to filter and flush out any bacteria that may be lingering in the faucet.

Yes, countertop reverse osmosis systems are worth it for households seeking to remove dissolved contaminants like lead and fluoride and who prefer a plumbing-free setup. However, they generally cost more and require more maintenance than pitchers or carbon-filter-only units, so they’re best when your water test or local report identifies concerns simpler filters can’t address.

Filter replacement timing varies by system and filter type, so it’s best to follow the manufacturer’s schedule for your specific system. Generally speaking, pitcher and faucet units may need new filters every few months, while countertop RO filters and membranes may last anywhere from 6 months to 2 years. You may need to replace filters sooner if the flow slows noticeably or your water develops an unusual taste or odor.

Michelle Larson has been a writer and editor for more than 10 years in the fields of health, business, and the home. Because she’d rather spend a little more up front than buy a tool or appliance twice, she strongly believes in the power of testing for finding quality items that are meant to last.

#7703. Sneezing After You Put Up the Tree? You Might Have Christmas Tree Syndrome

A Christmas tree may explain those December sniffles. Learn what Christmas tree syndrome feels like and how to reduce common triggers at home.

Being at home during the holidays can be a magical time of year for many. But for some, it also means dealing with allergies. Christmas tree syndrome could be responsible. Sneezing might start soon after the Christmas decorations go up, sometimes happening around the same time every year.

Dr. Racheal Onah, ND, consulting physician with RealTime Labs, explains what causes it, which symptoms to watch for, and how families can reduce their exposure.

Christmas tree syndrome refers to allergy and asthma symptoms that appear after putting up a Christmas tree or holiday decorations. Onah explains that the term is a nickname, not an official diagnosis, though the reactions are real.

Real Christmas trees can bring mold, pollen, and other allergens into the house. A study published in the Annals of Allergy, Asthma & Immunology identified several types of mold on Christmas trees, including some that can cause allergies.

“Outdoors, molds play a part in nature by breaking down dead organic matter such as fallen leaves and dead trees, but indoors, mold growth should be avoided,” explains the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. “Molds reproduce by means of tiny spores; the spores are invisible to the naked eye and float through outdoor and indoor air.”

Symptoms can include, but are not limited to:

Symptoms that get worse around the tree but improve away from home may point to an allergy. Onah says frequent sneezing and itchy eyes without a fever suggest an allergic reaction rather than a virus. A cold is more likely to bring a fever, sore throat, or body aches.

Onah suggests checking for mold or musty smells before buying a real tree. She recommends having the tree lot shake off loose debris, then rinsing the tree outside and letting it dry before bringing it indoors. Once inside, Onah recommends keeping the tree away from heating vents and running a HEPA air purifier in the same room.

Artificial trees can cause problems, too, depending on where and how they’re stored.

“Artificial trees that sat in a garage or basement for 11 months have had plenty of time to collect dust and moisture,” says Onah. “They are often stored in the original cardboard boxes they came in, which is a material that holds onto humidity and can feed mold on its own.”

Wreaths, garlands, and fabric decorations can collect dust or develop mold in storage as well. Scented candles and artificial snow sprays may also bother people with allergies.

Onah recommends unpacking decorations outside and wiping down artificial branches before setting them up. She says glass, metal, and hard plastic ornaments can be washed with warm water and mild dish soap. Porous decorations with visible mold or a musty smell, such as fabric, paper, or wood pieces, should be thrown away.

“When the season is over, make sure everything is completely dry before you pack it away,” says Onah. “Use sealed plastic bins instead of cardboard, add a few silica gel packets to absorb moisture, and store everything off the floor. If possible, opt to store your bins in a climate-controlled space like an interior closet rather than a garage, attic or basement.”

Anyone dealing with recurring allergy symptoms or worsening asthma should check with a healthcare provider.

“I’d pay extra attention if symptoms linger after the decorations come down,” says Onah. “This could be a sign the decor stirred up a bigger mold problem in the home, like a damp storage area or an HVAC system that’s harboring growth.”

#7699. Dupray Bloom Review: A HEPA Air Purifier Worth Putting on Display

Black Friday Deals Are Already Here ➡️ Tools, Generators, Essentials & More

Published Nov 24, 2026 12:36 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

I’ve tested a lot of air purifiers, and most look like appliances I’d rather tuck out of sight in a corner. The Dupray Bloom Air Purifier is different. It combines a HEPA air purifier with a removable planter, turning something purely functional into a decorative accent. I planted a small fiddle-leaf fig in mine, and I love how it looks in the room. But I also wanted to know whether the Bloom’s unusual design would interfere with its primary job of filtering the air.

Absolutely, and that’s what makes the Bloom so appealing. The top features a removable planting pot with a root tray that helps keep roots above excess water. I chose a small fiddle-leaf fig, and once it was planted, the Bloom looked more like a decorative planter than an air-cleaning appliance.

There is one thing I’d caution buyers about: The planter doesn’t have drainage holes. The root tray provides some separation from standing water, but it isn’t a substitute for proper watering. I’d recommend using an olla, a small porous automatic watering vessel that slowly releases moisture into the soil. It’s a good option for keeping the plant watered without repeatedly pouring water into a pot that can’t drain.

I also appreciated that the planter lifts completely out. That means I can move the plant for maintenance or repotting without having to move the entire purifier. And when it’s time to replace the round HEPA filter, I can remove the planter, turn the unit over, and access the filter from the bottom.

Behind its decorative design, the Bloom is a serious air purifier. It uses an H13 HEPA filter with activated carbon to capture airborne particles, including dust, pollen, and pet dander, while helping reduce odors. Dupray rates it as capable of capturing 99.97 percent of particles as small as 0.1 micron.

One feature I particularly liked was the stretchy fabric prefilter. It slips snugly over the purifier’s base, creating a smooth, modern appearance while catching larger airborne particles before they reach the HEPA filter. It’s washable, too, and Dupray offers replacement prefilters in different colors.

The Bloom also has an AutoDetect mode that monitors air quality and adjusts the fan speed. There are three manual fan settings, along with a sleep mode for quieter operation. Dupray rates its lowest noise level at just 24 decibels, making it suitable for bedrooms and other living spaces where a loud fan would be distracting.

It’s remarkably simple. The removable planter makes the HEPA filter accessible, and the fabric prefilter stretches on and off without clips or complicated fasteners.

Another smart touch is the universal power adapter. It comes with interchangeable plug configurations for the U.S., U.K., and Europe. That’s not something I typically see included with an air purifier.

My only complaint—and it’s minor—is the digital control display. The symbols for Auto, Sleep, and the fan-speed bars looked slightly blurry to me. I could still identify them and operate the purifier, but a sharper display would have been easier to read. Or I might need a new prescription for glasses.

At $249.99, the Bloom isn’t the cheapest way to get HEPA filtration, but its design sets it apart from the usual boxy models. It’s particularly appealing for living rooms, bedrooms, and home offices where an ordinary air purifier might detract from the decor.

Dupray advertises coverage up to 1,517 square feet, but that’s based on just one air change per hour. For more frequent air cleaning, it’s rated to cover 316 square feet at 4.8 air changes per hour. I’d use that smaller figure when choosing where to place it.

The Bloom also offers an optional wood tabletop model for anyone who prefers an accent table instead of a planter.

I love having a living plant incorporated into an appliance I’d otherwise try to hide. The Bloom is one of the few air purifiers I’ve tested that I’d happily put on display.

An official website of the United States government

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

Elias Shabazz, 33, of Los Angeles, was sentenced in the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California to 292 months in prison and five years of supervised release after being found guilty by a jury on June 26 of sex trafficking by force, fraud, or coercion. He was also ordered to pay $108,000 in restitution.

“This sentence reflects the cruelty of the defendant’s conduct in using physical and sexual violence and psychological coercion to compel commercial sex acts for his own financial gain,” said Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Justice Department’s Criminal Division. “The defendant treated the survivor of his abuse like a commodity for him to sell to commercial sex buyers. Today’s sentence ensures that Elias Shabazz will not victimize anyone else.”

“Shabazz used violence, threats, and coercion to force his victim into commercial sex, even firing a gun at her feet while threatening to kill her,” said First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli for the Central District of California. “He treated her life as a source of profit and used fear to maintain control. We will aggressively prosecute sex traffickers and seek substantial prison sentences for those who brutalize and exploit others.”

“Today's sentence delivers long-overdue accountability for Elias Shabazz’s calculated and vicious exploitation, in which he used brutality, terror, and control to turn a human being’s suffering into his personal source of income. It delivers a measure of justice to the survivor, prevents the defendant from inflicting further harm, and sends an unmistakable message that those who traffic and brutalize vulnerable people will face severe consequences,” said Acting Special Agent in Charge Kai Wah Chan of the Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) Washington, D.C. Field Office. “HSI Washington, D.C., together with our law enforcement partners, remains steadfast in working every day to identify traffickers, pursue them relentlessly, support survivors, and safeguard our communities from these predatory crimes.”

“This case highlights a core mission of HSI: preventing crimes of exploitation,” said Special Agent in Charge Erin Burke of HSI Los Angeles. “HSI is determined to rescue victims from exploitation and ensure that those who commit such cruel and violent acts are held accountable. The defendant manipulated and terrorized the victim for his own gain, using violence, intimidation, and control. The victim showed great bravery by coming forward and helping us with the investigation. HSI, together with our law enforcement partners, will continue to pursue justice for victims and relentlessly work to prevent these crimes from occurring in our communities.”

According to court documents, witness testimony, and evidence presented at trial, Elias Shabazz led his victim to believe that they were engaged in a romantic relationship, but he soon turned physically and sexually violent, demanding that the victim engage in commercial sex acts. Shabazz carried a handgun with him and used it on occasion to pistol whip the victim. He also fired the gun at her feet when threatening to kill her. At trial, the victim bravely testified to how Shabazz introduced her to commercial sex, demanded she meet a daily quota of commercial sex proceeds, and how he threatened her with the consequences of not meeting that quota. She also testified to how Shabazz compelled her to work on Figueroa Street in Los Angeles and how dangerous it was. Shabazz confiscated the victim’s identification, social security card, and birth certificate, and constantly looked through her phone to keep her from communicating with family and friends. He also introduced her to addictive narcotics and controlled every aspect of her life including when she ate, slept, and showered.

The jury convicted Shabazz of one count of sex trafficking by force, fraud, or coercion.

Trial Attorney Kate A. Alexander of the Criminal Division’s Human Rights and Special Prosecutions Section and Assistant U.S. Attorney Karen I. Meyer for the Central District of California are prosecuting the case.

Anyone who has information about human trafficking should report that information to the National Human Trafficking Hotline toll-free at 1-888-373-7888, which is available 24 hours a day, seven days a week. For more information about human trafficking, please visit www.humantraffickinghotline.org. Information on the Justice Department’s efforts to combat human trafficking can be found at www.justice.gov/humantrafficking.
